title: Fertilizer

definition.text: Any natural or synthetic material applied to soil or to plant tissues to supply plant nutrients.

facts.text: Fertilizers can be distinguished from liming materials and other soil amendments that supply no nutrients.
Modern fertilization centres on three macronutrients, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, occasionally with supplements such as rock flour for micronutrients.
Fertilizers boost plant growth mainly by supplying nutrients; some also act by improving the soil's water-holding capacity and aeration.
Before synthetic products, fertility came from compost, animal and human manure, mined minerals, crop rotations and by-products such as fish waste or bloodmeal.
Application rates depend on the crop and on soil fertility, usually measured by a soil test; legumes fix their own nitrogen and generally need no nitrogen fertilizer.
Conservative estimates attribute 30 to 50% of crop yields to natural or synthetic commercial fertilizers.
Agriculture used 190 million tonnes of inorganic fertilizer nutrients in 2023, of which 112 million tonnes (58%) was nitrogen.
Excessive use can pollute water through nutrient runoff and eutrophication, and some mined fertilizers add heavy metals to soil.

title: History of fertilizers

definition.text: The development of fertilizer use from ancient manuring and minerals to the synthetic fertilizer industry that grew from the 19th century.

facts.text: Early farmers may have manured crops as long as 8,000 years ago; Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans are recorded using minerals or manure.
Andean farmers used guano for at least 1,500 years before 19th-century Europe and the USA imported it in quantity from Peru and Chile.
Justus von Liebig, often called the father of the fertilizer industry, attacked Thaer's humus theory and stressed ammonia and then inorganic minerals in plant nutrition.
John Bennet Lawes began testing manures on potted plants in 1837 and in 1842 patented a manure of phosphates treated with sulfuric acid, founding the artificial manure industry.
Lawes and Joseph Henry Gilbert founded the Rothamsted station, which still studies how inorganic and organic fertilizers affect crop yields.
Industrial nitrogen fertilizer began with processes such as Birkeland–Eyde, which fixed atmospheric nitrogen into nitric acid; the Haber and Ostwald processes rose in the 1910s and 1920s.
Nitrogen fertilizer use grew 800% between 1961 and 2019, a crucial part of the Green Revolution's productivity gains.
Phosphate fertilizer use rose from 9 million tonnes a year in 1960 to 40 million tonnes in 2000.

notes: Re-anchored on the dedicated page History of fertilizer; WWII and Lawes–Gilbert facts moved to mentions.

definition.text: The nutrients fertilizers supply in varying proportions: chiefly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK), plus micronutrients.

facts.text: Nitrogen supports leaf and stem growth; phosphorus root, flower, seed and fruit development; potassium strong stems, water movement, flowering and fruiting.
Nutrients are not applied as pure elements; fertilizers are made of compounds that contain them.
Macronutrients make up 0.15% to 6.0% of plant dry matter, and plants take up more than they need (luxury consumption) when overfertilized.
Nitrogen is the most important fertilizer element, being part of proteins, DNA and chlorophyll; atmospheric nitrogen is abundant but in a form plants cannot use.
Plants obtain nitrogen through weathering of nitrogen-bearing rocks and through fixation by some free-living and symbiotic bacteria, notably in legume roots.
Phosphate is needed for DNA, the energy carrier ATP and the phospholipids of cell membranes.
Calcium, long thought a luxury, is now considered essential for keeping plant cell walls and membranes intact.

title: Fertilizer classification

definition.text: The grouping of fertilizers by how many nutrients they supply, straight or multinutrient, and by origin, inorganic or organic.

facts.text: Straight fertilizers supply a single nutrient such as N, P or K; multinutrient or complex fertilizers supply two or more.
Inorganic fertilizers exclude carbon-bearing materials except urea and are also called synthetic, because chemical treatments are needed to make them.
Organic fertilizers are usually recycled plant- or animal-derived matter such as compost or manure.
NP fertilizers such as monoammonium phosphate (11% N, 48% P2O5) and diammonium phosphate (18% N, 46% P2O5) supply both nitrogen and phosphorus.
NPK fertilizers supply all three main nutrients: compound NPKs bind them chemically, while blends are physical mixtures of single-nutrient fertilizers.
Solubility varies: more than 90% of a typical superphosphate dissolves in water, against about 85% of MAP and DAP.

notes: The 'Single nutrient (straight) fertilizers' and 'Multinutrient fertilizers' subsections are folded in here and into the nitrogen, phosphate and potassium entries.

title: NPK rating

definition.text: A label of three numbers giving a fertilizer's content of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

facts.text: The numbers, separated by dashes as in 10-10-10, give the percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O.
Fertilizers contain no actual P2O5 or K2O; the oxides are a conventional shorthand for their phosphorus and potassium.
UK rules allow the elemental phosphorus and potassium values in parentheses after the standard figures, as in 15-30-15 (15-13-13).
Australia uses an N-P-K-S system that adds a fourth number for sulfur and gives elemental values for all nutrients.

distinct_from: Converting NPK labels to elemental content

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply elements plants need only in tiny amounts, typically boron, zinc, molybdenum, iron and manganese.

facts.text: Micronutrients occur in plant tissue at 0.15 to 400 ppm, less than 0.04% of dry matter, yet as enzyme co-factors their impact far exceeds their concentration.
They are supplied as water-soluble salts; iron is often given as a chelate such as EDTA or EDDHA, since at moderate pH and phosphate it turns insoluble.
Needs depend on plant and setting: sugar beets need boron and legumes cobalt, while heat or drought makes boron less available.
Zinc deficiency is common in soils worldwide, affecting both plants and people, and zinc fertilizers are widely used against it.

title: Nitrogen fertilizers

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply nitrogen, made from ammonia produced by the Haber–Bosch process.

facts.text: In this energy-intensive process natural gas usually supplies the hydrogen and the air supplies the nitrogen.
The ammonia is the feedstock for other nitrogen fertilizers such as ammonium nitrate and urea; nitrates are also made from it by the Ostwald process.
Common straight nitrogen fertilizers include ammonium nitrate with 34-35% nitrogen and calcium ammonium nitrate, a limestone or dolomite blend with 24-28% nitrogen.
Sodium nitrate (Chilean saltpeter) from the Atacama Desert was one of the original nitrogen fertilizers, used from 1830, and is still mined.
About a third of annual global food production uses Haber–Bosch ammonia, supporting nearly half the world's population.
Nitrogen fertilizer was used at about 110 million tons of nitrogen a year in 2012.
Only part of the nitrogen applied becomes plant matter; the rest accumulates in the soil or is lost as runoff.
In soil, bacteria such as Nitrosomonas oxidize ammonia to nitrite and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate, which is highly soluble and easily leached.

related: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle

title: Phosphate fertilizers

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply phosphorus, extracted from phosphate rock whose main minerals are fluorapatite and hydroxyapatite.

facts.text: Acid treatment turns the rock's minerals into water-soluble phosphate salts; this use is the main reason so much sulfuric acid is made.
The main straight phosphate fertilizers are superphosphates: single superphosphate has 14–18% P2O5 plus phosphogypsum, triple superphosphate 44–48% P2O5 and no gypsum.
Billions of kilograms of phosphate rock are mined each year, but the remaining ore is shrinking in size and quality, making future supply a critical issue.
Each ton of phosphoric acid made from phosphate rock leaves five tons of phosphogypsum, an impure radioactive waste; 100 to 280 million tons are produced yearly.
A maize crop yielding 6–9 tonnes of grain per hectare needs 31–50 kg of phosphate fertilizer, and soybeans about half, 20–25 kg per hectare.
Phosphate, normally a limiting nutrient, is the main contributor to eutrophication, since high concentrations promote the growth of cyanobacteria and algae.

title: Potassium fertilizers

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply potassium, made from potash, a mixture of potassium minerals.

facts.text: Potassium is the third major crop nutrient after nitrogen and phosphorus, and about 90% of potash goes to fertilizer.
The main potassium straight fertilizer is muriate of potash, 95–99% potassium chloride; others are potassium sulfate, carbonate or nitrate.
Potassium content is reported as K2O equivalent for comparison, though plants do not take up K2O and the fertilizers contain none.
The name comes from pot ash: plant or wood ashes soaked in water in a pot, the main way potash was made before the industrial era.
Potash ores are natural mixtures of sylvite (potassium chloride) and halite; mined ore is processed to separate KCl into a high-analysis potassium fertilizer.
World production exceeded 71.9 million tonnes in 2021, Canada producing most; China, the United States, Brazil and India are the largest consumers.
Potash improves the water retention, yield, nutrient value, taste, colour, texture and disease resistance of food crops.
Manure and glauconite (greensand) are low-potassium sources that pay to transport only short distances.

definition.text: Fertilizers of biological origin, derived from living or formerly living materials.

facts.text: They include animal wastes, crop wastes, seaweed, compost and treated sewage sludge (biosolids), plus slaughter by-products such as bloodmeal, bone meal and feather meal.
The term also covers packaged products meeting organic farming rules, which limit or avoid synthetic fertilizers and pesticides.
Sewage sludge may be unacceptable in organic farming because of residual contaminants and public perception.
Most hold less-concentrated nutrients that are harder to quantify, but they can offer soil-building advantages.
Compost and similar materials can raise nutrient availability by improving cation-exchange capacity or by boosting microorganisms that free nutrients.
Peat, the most used packaged organic amendment, improves aeration and moisture but adds no nutrients, so it is an amendment rather than a fertilizer.
Fresh sawdust can draw down soil nitrogen as wood-decay fungi colonize it, a property that can also capture excess mineral nitrogen.
Their nutrient content, solubility and release rates are typically much lower than mineral fertilizers', which can make them slow-release and lessen the risk of over-fertilization.

definition.text: Matching when and how much fertilizer is applied to crop needs, weather and the type of farming.

facts.text: Timing applications to peak nutrient demand is essential for yield and quality; uptake peaks from early to mid-season, so fertilizing near seeding works well.
For fall-planted grains such as winter wheat, autumn nitrogen followed by spring topdressing is likely the best combination.
Soluble fertilizers such as ammonium nitrate are not applied during heavy rain, which would carry most of it away and pollute the aquifer.
Conservation agriculture and smallholdings cut mineral fertilizer to the crop's strict needs, sometimes to none.
After harvest, a fast-growing, nitrogen-hungry catch crop such as white mustard can take up leftover nitrate before it reaches groundwater, then be buried to form humus.

title: Solid and liquid fertilizers

definition.text: The two physical forms in which fertilizers reach crops: granules, powders or prills, or water-based solutions.

facts.text: About 90% of fertilizers are applied as solids, most commonly urea, diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride.
Liquid fertilizers are solutions of ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea; they act faster and cover more evenly, while granules are cheaper to ship, store and apply.
Adding fertilizer to irrigation water is called fertigation, used mostly on high-value crops such as vegetables, turf, fruit trees and ornamentals.
Fertigation places nutrients where the water goes and allows small doses, reducing fertilizer use and leaching.

notes: Fertigation now has its own entry; the two fertigation facts here stay as context for liquid application.

title: Nitrification and urease inhibitors

definition.text: Chemicals added to nitrogen fertilizers to slow their conversion in the soil and so make them more efficient.

facts.text: Nitrification inhibitors, also called nitrogen stabilizers, suppress the biological oxidation of ammonia into nitrate, an anion more prone to leaching.
Urease inhibitors such as NBPT, added to urea fertilizers at 0.05 weight percent, slow urea's enzymatic hydrolysis into ammonia, which can evaporate or be nitrified.
A stabilized nitrogen fertilizer carries an added stabilizer that keeps its nitrogen in the soil longer in urea or ammonium form.
Using them lets farmers limit the polluting effects of nitrogen runoff.

definition.text: The direct and indirect harm that producing and using fertilizers does to water, soil, air and ecosystems.

facts.text: Direct effects include runoff that causes ocean dead zones and contaminates waterways, degradation of the soil microbiome and accumulation of toxic compounds.
The IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land names fertilizer production and associated land use among the drivers of global warming.
Indirect impacts include nitrogen-crop-pest cascades, fracking for Haber process gas, and biodiversity loss and soil loss tied to industrial agriculture.
Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, with methane supplying hydrogen for ammonia; solar energy, waste treatment and electrolysis are proposed alternatives.
Excessive organic amendments such as pig slurry can also contaminate aquifers and eutrophy the waters they feed.
Policy responses favour sustainable or regenerative farming with less synthetic fertilizer, better soil management and more organic fertilizer.
Practices such as reduced tillage and buffer strips can lessen these effects.

title: Fertilizer runoff and water pollution

definition.text: The movement of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized land into surface water with rain and snowmelt, and into groundwater by leaching.

facts.text: Agricultural runoff is a major contributor to freshwater eutrophication, mainly through phosphate, which feeds algae and cyanobacteria whose decay uses up oxygen.
Nitrogen-rich runoff is the primary cause of serious oxygen depletion in coastal zones, lakes and rivers, and coastal dead zones are increasing.
Much of the nitrogen that plants do not take up, whether from synthetic or natural fertilizer, turns into easily leached nitrate; groundwater above 10 mg/L can cause blue baby syndrome.
Even where eutrophication can be reversed, decades and much soil management may pass before natural denitrification clears accumulated groundwater nitrate.

notes: Covers both the Water section and its Nitrate pollution subsection.

title: Acidification by nitrogen fertilizers

definition.text: The lowering of soil pH caused by the ammonium and nitrate that nitrogen fertilizers release as they react in the soil.

facts.text: Mineral or organic nitrogen fertilizers raise the concentration of hydrogen ions in the soil solution, lowering soil pH.
Acidification causes cation leaching, unstable aggregates, metal toxicity and lower nutrient availability, harming soil life and crops.
The loss of nutrient availability can be offset by liming, which also counteracts the acidification caused by plant growth and crop removal of nutrients.
In intensive farming regions nitrogen fertilizers also feed acid rain, through ammonia volatilized from manure or urea and nitrogen oxides redeposited as nitric acid.

title: Toxic elements in fertilizers

definition.text: Contaminants such as cadmium, fluoride, uranium and other heavy metals that some fertilizers, especially phosphate and slag-based ones, add to soils.

facts.text: Cadmium varies widely: monoammonium phosphate can hold from 0.14 to 50.9 mg/kg, and phosphate rock up to 188 mg/kg.
Continued use of high-cadmium fertilizer can contaminate soils and plants, so producers now choose phosphate rock by its cadmium content.
Phosphate rock is rich in fluoride, so phosphate fertilizers have raised soil fluoride; plants take up little, so the greater concern is livestock that eat contaminated soil.
Uranium-238 runs from 7 to 100 pCi/g in phosphate rock and 1 to 67 pCi/g in phosphate fertilizers; heavy use can raise levels in soils and drainage water several-fold.
The added health risk from radionuclides in food is very small, less than 0.05 mSv/y.
Steel slag, recycled as an amendment for its calcium, magnesium and trace elements, can carry arsenic, cadmium, chromium and nickel, though it helps immobilize lead.
Mixing biochar into steel slag makes a good amendment for immobilizing heavy metals in farm soils.

title: Trace mineral depletion

definition.text: The question of why concentrations of micronutrients such as iron, zinc, copper and magnesium in many foods have fallen over the last 50–60 years.

facts.text: Intensive farming with synthetic fertilizers is often blamed, and organic farming is often proposed as the remedy.
Higher NPK-driven yields dilute other nutrients, but much of the decline is attributed to higher-yielding crop varieties with lower mineral concentrations.
Fertilizers more often cure trace deficiencies: zinc, copper, manganese, iron and molybdenum shortages found in Western Australia in the 1940s and 1950s are now corrected routinely.

contested_note: Synthetic fertilizers are often blamed for falling micronutrient levels in food, but the source attributes most of the decline to higher-yielding crop varieties.

title: Fertilizer effects on soil biology

definition.text: The changes heavy fertilizer use brings to soil organisms, from root symbioses to soil animals and microbes.

facts.text: High fertilizer levels, especially beyond plant needs, can break down the symbiosis between plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi.
Organic and organic–mineral fertilizers increase soil fauna abundance while mineral fertilizers do not, and chemical fertilizers boost microbial growth without changing diversity.
Acid stress combined with high nitrogen, rare before industrial agriculture, weakens links between aboveground and belowground parts of agroecosystems.
Nitrogen deposition is turning Sphagnum bogs from carbon sinks into carbon sources by stimulating decomposers.

contested_note: Whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals is still debated, with group-specific responses masking overall effects.

title: Fertilizers and greenhouse gases

definition.text: The carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide released in making and using nitrogen fertilizer, estimated at around 5% of human greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: About one third of these emissions comes from production and two thirds from fertilizer use.
Soil bacteria convert nitrate to nitrous oxide, the third most important greenhouse gas, 296 times stronger per ton than carbon dioxide and a contributor to ozone depletion.
Human nitrous oxide emissions, mostly from fertilizer, were estimated at 700 million tons of CO2 equivalent between 2007 and 2016.
Ammonium-based fertilizers increase methane emissions from crop fields, notably rice paddies.

related: Effects of climate change on agriculture

title: Urea

definition.text: A simple organic nitrogen compound, CO(NH2)2, found in mammal urine and widely used as a nitrogen fertilizer.

facts.text: More than 90% of the world's industrial urea is used as a nitrogen-release fertilizer.
With 45-46% nitrogen it has the highest nitrogen content of common solid nitrogen fertilizers, so it is cheap to transport per unit of nitrogen, and it is non-explosive.
Soil bacteria with the enzyme urease convert it to ammonium, which roots take up; in some soils bacteria then oxidize the ammonium to nitrate.
Because nitrogen lost to air and runoff is wasteful and harmful, urea is coated in inert sealants or converted to urea-formaldehyde compounds that release nitrogen slowly.
Biuret, the most common impurity in synthetic urea, impairs plant growth.
Where it is cheap, urea is used to reduce soil alkalinity: ammonium from its hydrolysis displaces sodium from the soil's exchange sites.
Urea runoff from fertilized land may help make algal blooms toxic.
In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from inorganic starting materials, contradicting the doctrine of vitalism.

title: Controlled-release fertiliser

definition.text: A granulated fertilizer that releases its nutrients into the soil gradually, over a controlled period.

facts.text: It is also called controlled-availability, delayed-release, metered-release or slow-acting fertilizer, and usually supplies nitrogen.
Conventional fertilizers dissolve and disperse; controlled-release ones are not water-soluble, so their nutrients reach the soil more slowly.
Release rate is set by low solubility in soil moisture, the breakdown of pellet coatings, and conversion of the chemicals into ammonia or another usable nutrient.
Most slow-release types are urea derivatives: urea-formaldehyde, first made in 1936 and sold from 1955, and IBDU slowly convert to urea in the soil.
Coated types wrap ordinary fertilizer in sulfur or plastic; sulfur-coated urea releases as soil microbes degrade the sealant and through cracks, typically over 6 to 16 weeks in turf.
On average 16% of conventional nitrogen fertilizer is lost as ammonia, nitrous oxide or nitrogen gas or in runoff, so slower release aims at more efficient use.
Controlled release protects crops from fertilizer burn, needs fewer applications and less fertilizer, and in most cases improves yield by more than 10%.
It can reduce nitrogen pollution behind eutrophication and nitrous oxide emissions, which arise when microbes act on ammonia faster than plants absorb it.

definition.text: Organic matter, mostly animal feces, used as organic fertilizer in agriculture.

facts.text: Most manure is animal feces; compost and green manure are the other two main classes used in soil management today.
Manures build fertility by adding organic matter and nutrients such as nitrogen that feed soil bacteria and fungi, which in turn feed the rest of the soil food web.
Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans are all recorded using manure or minerals to make farms more productive.
The term artificial manure, once in wide use, meant what are now called artificial fertilizers.
Adding manure, like compost or mulch, can change a soil's carbon-to-nitrogen ratio.
Long manuring leaves a mark in the profile: anthrosols of northwestern Europe often have plaggic or terric horizons, covering some 500,000 hectares.
Manure is also composted, bagged and sold as a soil amendment.

title: Animal manure

definition.text: Manure made from livestock dung and urine, handled either as farmyard manure mixed with bedding or as liquid slurry.

facts.text: Farmyard manure includes straw bedding that has soaked up feces and urine; slurry is the liquid form from intensive units using concrete or slats instead of straw.
Manures from horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, poultry and other animals, and guano from seabirds and bats, differ in quality and need different application rates.
Sheep manure is high in nitrogen and potash and pig manure relatively low in both; cattle manure supplies nitrogen and organic carbon, and chicken litter is rich in nitrogen and phosphate.
Animal manure improves soil aggregation so the soil holds more water and nutrients, and it stimulates microbes that improve the supply of trace minerals.
Poultry droppings harm plants when fresh but become valuable fertilizer after composting.
Horse manure can carry grass and weed seeds, because horses do not digest seeds as cattle do.
Strong-smelling slurries, such as those from intensive pig farms, are usually injected into the soil to limit odour; pig and cattle manure is normally spread with a manure spreader.

title: Hazards of animal manure

definition.text: The health and environmental risks of animal manure, from pathogens and nitrogen losses to drug residues taken up by crops.

facts.text: Any manure can carry pathogens or food-spoilage organisms, spread by flies, rodents and other vectors, that threaten food safety.
Under intensive land use manure is applied less precisely than mineral fertilizer, so its nitrogen is used poorly, and it can emit the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide.
In 2007 a University of Minnesota study found corn, lettuce and potatoes taking up antibiotics from soils spread with manure containing these drugs.
Organic farming standards require non-organic manure to be rotted or composted first, to break down drug residues and kill pathogenic bacteria.

definition.text: A crop grown specifically to be worked into the soil while still green.

facts.text: Its biomass is ploughed or disced in, as with ordinary manure, mainly to add organic matter to the soil.
Green manuring often uses legumes such as clover and vetch, whose root-nodule bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, a natural fertilizer for the next crop, in organic and conventional farming alike.
Depending on the species, 45 to 224 kg/ha (40 to 200 lb/acre) of nitrogen is released, and usually 40-60% of the crop's nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.
As it decays it also releases phosphorus, potassium and sulfur, and deep-rooted species bring up nutrients shallower crops cannot reach.
Added organic matter and microbial mycelium and sticky substances improve aggregation, infiltration, water retention and aeration, and its roots can penetrate compacted soil.
While growing it suppresses weeds, helps control erosion, feeds pollinators, shelters beneficial insects and can reduce some pests and diseases.
Green manure also lowers the pH of alkali soils by generating humic acid.
Greek farmers ploughed beans into the soil by about 300 BC and the Romans used faba beans and lupines; colonists took the practice to North America.

definition.text: The breakdown of incorporated green manure by heterotrophic bacteria into nutrients available to the following crop.

facts.text: Warmth and moisture drive the process, as in composting, and the decaying matter gives off carbon dioxide and weak acids that free nutrients from insoluble minerals.
On soils rich in calcium minerals, green manure can raise the phosphate content.
The plant's carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, which varies with species and age, must be below 30:1 or decomposing bacteria will deplete soil nitrogen and starve the crop.
Working green manure in too short a time before planting can cause nitrogen immobilization, leaving too little for the next crop.

definition.text: A mixture of decomposed organic materials used as plant fertilizer and to improve the soil's physical, chemical and biological properties.

facts.text: It is made by decomposing plant and food waste, recycled organic materials and manure, and is rich in nutrients and organisms such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes and fungi.
Compost feeds crops, conditions the soil, raises its humus or humic acid content, and adds microbes that suppress pathogens and soil-borne diseases.
It adds organic matter to the soil and increases both its nutrient content and the biodiversity of its microbes.
Compost improves fertility in gardens, horticulture, urban agriculture and organic farming, reducing dependence on chemical fertilizers.
Food and other compostables make up about 20% of landfill waste; composting them avoids the methane released when they decay without oxygen in landfills.
Compost is also used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction and landfill cover, and composting in biopiles and windrows is a bioremediation technique.
Alkaline soils containing solid calcium carbonate can be reclaimed by working in compost and other acidifying organic materials.
Composting dates back at least to the early Roman Empire, described by Cato the Elder in 160 BCE; the first industrial composting station opened in Wels, Austria, in 1921.

definition.text: The aerobic decomposition of organic solid wastes into a humus-like material, compost.

facts.text: Composting organisms need four ingredients: carbon for energy, whose oxidation gives heat; nitrogen to grow; oxygen to oxidize the carbon; and enough water without waterlogging.
Aerobic bacteria need oxygen above 5%, so heaps are turned to keep up oxygen and the right moisture.
Bacteria and fungi turn the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide and ammonium ions, and the materials become humus over months.
Composting is most efficient at a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of about 25:1; above 30 the mix is nitrogen-starved, and below 15 it tends to lose nitrogen as ammonia.
Green waste such as grass, leaves and food scraps supplies nitrogen and brown waste such as stalks, paper and wood chips carbon; fresh grass is about 15:1, dry autumn leaves about 50:1.
Balancing air and water keeps the heap at 130–160 °F (54–71 °C) until the materials are broken down.
On farms, manure is the usual nitrogen source and bedding such as straw or sawdust the carbon source; poultry manure needs blending with high-carbon materials and wet pig manure with straw.

definition.text: The chemical decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, and physical decomposers, such as worms and insects, that break down compost.

facts.text: Bacteria are the most abundant and important, excreting plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium; mesophilic or thermophilic kinds dominate depending on the phase.
Actinomycetota break down tough paper, bark, lignin and cellulose and give compost its earthy smell; fungi decompose woody material that bacteria cannot.
Earthworms eat partly composted material and excrete castings that make nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium available, while their tunnels improve aeration and drainage.
Thermophilic bacteria, inactive between −5 and 25 °C yet present throughout soil, activate once mesophiles warm the heap and thrive at 40–60 °C.

title: Phases of composting

definition.text: The sequence of temperature stages that composting passes through under ideal conditions, from mesophilic to thermophilic to cooling and maturation.

facts.text: In the first, mesophilic phase, microorganisms decompose the material at moderate temperatures.
As the heap warms, thermophilic bacteria take over at 50 to 60 °C (122 to 140 °F).
As high-energy compounds run out the temperature falls through a cooling and a maturation phase, and mesophilic bacteria cure the compost, making it more bioavailable to plants.
Semicomposting, of volumes too small for full composting, never reaches a thermophilic stage.

title: Hot and cold composting
article: Compost#Hot and cold composting – impact on timing

definition.text: Two ways of composting that differ in pile size and temperature, and so in how long they take.

facts.text: Composting time depends on the volume of material, the particle size of the inputs, and how much it is mixed and aerated.
In hot composting, the usual method of municipal and farm operations, large piles reach high temperatures and stay thermophilic for days or weeks.
The Berkeley method finishes compost in 18 days from at least 1 cubic metre of material, turned every two days after the first four, with C:N held at 30:1 or less.
Cold composting in piles under 1 cubic metre, such as most home heaps, can take up to a year; it needs no turning, but parts may go anaerobic.

definition.text: The killing of pathogens and weed seeds by the heat of composting, and the suppression of plant pathogens by finished compost.

facts.text: Stabilized compost that has reached 50–70 °C poses very little risk, since these temperatures kill pathogens and even make oocysts unviable.
The temperature that kills a pathogen depends on the organism, how long the heat lasts (seconds to weeks) and pH.

Compost teas and extracts inhibit crop pathogens such as Fusarium oxysporum, Rhizoctonia and Pythium, and compost supplies biocontrol agents such as Bacillus subtilis; sterilizing compost weakens this effect.
Compost that has not passed 50 °C should be turned wearing a respirator and gloves, against diseases such as aspergillosis, farmer's lung, Legionnaires' disease and tetanus.

definition.text: The use of finished compost on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients.

facts.text: On open fields compost is broadcast in a very thin layer, about 6 mm (0.24 in), and worked in before planting; 25 mm (0.98 in) or more is used to rebuild poor soils or control erosion.
Added to soil, coir or peat, it improves tilth and supplies humus and nutrients; tilled in, it raises organic matter and overall fertility.
It is rarely used alone but mixed with sand, grit, bark, vermiculite, perlite or clay granules; blends of 20–30% compost are common for transplanting seedlings.
Seeding directly into compost is not advised: it dries fast, immature compost may hold germination-inhibiting phytotoxins, and undecomposed lignin may tie up nitrogen.
Compost ready for use is dark brown or black with an earthy smell.
Compost can increase plant immunity to diseases and pests.

Finished compost supplies little readily available nitrogen, since composting converts much N to stable organic forms while P and K availability is unchanged; it still releases other nutrients slowly and raises organic matter.

Annual high rates set by nitrogen need overload soil with phosphorus and potassium, and salts may build up under high tunnels and greenhouses, so soil tests should guide a switch to legume cover crops.

title: Compost tea

definition.text: A liquid of fermented water extracts leached from composted materials, applied to crops.

facts.text: It is usually made by adding compost to water at 1:4–1:10 and stirring occasionally to release microbes, either with or without aeration.
Field studies show benefits from added organic matter, nutrient availability and microbial activity, and suppression of plant pathogens and soil-borne diseases.
Aerated tea brews faster with more microbes; non-aerated tea is cheaper, but studies conflict on its phytotoxicity and pathogen risks, and added nutrients can regrow E. coli and Salmonella.
Compost extracts are unbrewed, unfermented extracts in any solvent; aerated compost teas suppress pathogens more effectively than extracts.

contested_note: Sources report debate over the benefits of aerating compost tea and conflicting studies on the risks of non-aerated tea.

title: Industrial composting

definition.text: Large-scale composting methods, chiefly in-vessel, aerated static-pile and windrow composting.

facts.text: In-vessel composting confines material in tanks or bunkers where airflow and temperature are controlled as in a bioreactor; it treats sewage biosolids, food waste and municipal organics.
In-vessel systems sanitize pathogens so the waste can be reclaimed as a soil amendment, while limiting odours, runoff and emissions.
Aerated static piles are kept aerobic by forcing air through perforated pipes instead of turning; roofs reduce leachate.
Windrow composting piles manure, crop residues and other wastes in long rows; such large operations can get hot enough to kill beneficial microbes while pasteurizing the waste.

notes: Named manufacturers and products in the in-vessel subsection skipped.

definition.text: Human excreta used as a nutrient-rich input to composting.

facts.text: In soil it builds organic matter and healthy microbial communities; feces supply nitrogen, urine phosphorus, and both are a good source of potassium.
Feces can carry bacteria, viruses and parasitic worms, but proper fermentation kills pathogens and parasite eggs within two weeks to six months, depending on climate.
Urine added to compost raises its temperature, helping destroy pathogens and seeds, and unlike feces it does not attract flies or carry worm eggs.
The term was coined by organic farmer Joseph Jenkins.

definition.text: A dry toilet that treats human waste by composting, turning it into a compost-like material.

facts.text: Most use no flush water; a carbon additive such as sawdust, coir or peat moss is added after each use, making air pockets, improving the C:N ratio and reducing odour.
Most rely on mesophilic composting; long retention or a secondary composting step kills more pathogens and gives a humus-like product that can enrich soil where rules allow.
Nutrients in composting-toilet compost are more plant-available than in dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets.
Using composting-toilet compost in one's own garden is regarded as safe, though legal restrictions may apply because pathogens can survive.

title: Vermicompost

definition.text: The product of composting with worms: a mix of decomposing food or plant waste, bedding and worm castings (vermicast).

facts.text: Red wigglers (Eisenia fetida or E. andrei) are the usual worms; composting worms are surface-dwelling epigeic species, while burrowing anecic Lumbricus species adapt poorly to shallow bins.
Worm castings hold fewer contaminants and more concentrated nutrients than the original materials.
It treats organic wastes faster than conventional composting, and vermicomposted manure has lower salinity and a more neutral pH.
It is richer in many nutrients than other composts, and the worm mucus coating castings slows nutrient release and keeps nutrients from washing away.
Microbial activity in worm castings is 10 to 20 times higher than in the soil and organic matter the worm eats.
Redworms feed fastest at 15–25 °C, survive 10 °C and may be harmed above 30 °C; bin moisture must stay above 50%, ideally 70–80%.
It can be mixed into soil or steeped as worm tea; the leachate draining from bins is different, uncomposted and may carry pathogens.
Worms also treat sewage: vermifiltration cleans wastewater or blackwater, and vermicomposting follows urine-diverting dry toilets in terra preta sanitation.

title: Phosphate rich organic manure

definition.text: An organic fertilizer made by co-composting rock phosphate, used as an alternative to diammonium phosphate and single superphosphate.

facts.text: It is made by co-composting very finely ground (80% finer than 54 microns) high-grade rock phosphate of 32% ± 2% P2O5; the finer the rock, the better it works.
Rock phosphate holds its phosphorus as insoluble tricalcium phosphate; microbial organic acids slowly dissolve it, and the organic matter stops other ions locking phosphorus into insoluble forms.
Phosphorus dissolves best between pH 5.5 and 7: aluminium, iron and manganese hold pH below 5.5, and magnesium and calcium keep it above 7, both blocking release.
It may add phosphorus more efficiently than chemical fertilizers and feeds a second crop as well as the first; acidic waste solids from biogas plants can be used to make it.

title: Night soil

definition.text: A historical euphemism for human excreta collected, usually at night, from cesspools, privies, pail closets and pit latrines.

facts.text: It came from sanitation without sewers or septic tanks, collected undiluted by water, and was sometimes carted out of town and sold as fertilizer.
Using unprocessed feces as fertilizer is risky: parasitic worm infections such as ascariasis are linked to night soil use because the eggs pass from person to person in feces.
Proper fecal sludge management, such as composting, reduces these risks, and human excreta can be safely turned into compost.
Ancient Athens channelled its sewage to the Cephissus valley as fertilizer, Edo's compost merchants sold feces to farmers, and Aztec chinampas were built of mud and human waste.

notes: Country histories and manual-scavenging sections skipped as social history; S:e695daf2aba7 (Japan: under 1% of night soil now used as fertilizer) is another usable fact.

title: Reuse of human excreta

definition.text: The use of treated human excreta for the plant nutrients, organic matter and energy it contains, most often as fertilizer and soil conditioner.

facts.text: Reuse in agriculture 'closes the loop' between sanitation and farming and is central to ecological sanitation.
Excreta-derived fertilizers include urine, dried feces, composted feces, fecal sludge, sewage and sewage sludge, each with different fertilizing properties.
Treatments such as urine diversion and drying of feces, composting, and sewage or fecal sludge treatment remove pathogens to varying degrees and reduce water content.
In Africa the nutrients theoretically recoverable from excreta match all current fertilizer use, offering smallholders an alternative to often unaffordable chemical fertilizer.
Unlike mined phosphate fertilizers, which can carry cadmium and uranium into the food chain, excreta-based fertilizers generally lack these heavy metals.
Their nutrients are bound in organic compounds or adsorbed on humic acids, so they release slowly and leach less readily than mineral fertilizers.
Like other nitrogen fertilizers they can cause nitrate leaching, while pharmaceutical residues in excreta degrade better in soil than in water.
Excreta and sewage nutrients have been used in farming for centuries, but often in unregulated and unsafe ways in developing countries.

contested_note: The source says debate is ongoing about whether reuse of excreta is cost-effective.
notes: Definition line S:4edcbf3bff04 ('can be safe or unsafe') is not a definition; the definition is paraphrased from the lead. Contested flag from S:6eb4fbddb535. Fuel, building-material and country sections skipped.

definition.text: The use of human urine, rich in nitrogen (mostly as urea) and potassium, as a crop fertilizer.

facts.text: Urine carries about 70% of the nitrogen and more than half the potassium in sewage while making up less than 1% of its volume.
Design values are 4 kg nitrogen, 0.36 kg phosphorus and 1.0 kg potassium per person per year, about 7:1.5:2.2 as N:P2O5:K2O, varying with diet.
Its nitrogen content rises with the protein in the diet.
It is applied diluted, 1:5 for container crops or 1:8 for general use, because undiluted urine can burn leaves or roots, especially in dry soil.
Its fertilizing effect is comparable to commercial nitrogen fertilizers, and it holds far less lead, mercury and cadmium than sewage sludge.
Limits are excess nitrogen and salts such as sodium chloride; over-application can cause excess ammonia, acidity or other phytotoxicity.
In storage its urea is quickly hydrolyzed to ammonia; delivering it through perforated hoses about 10 cm below the surface cuts odour, volatilization and pathogen transfer.
Health risks are generally regarded as negligible, especially when urine is dispersed in soil rather than on edible plant parts.

title: Feces as fertilizer

definition.text: The use of treated human feces, dried, composted or as fecal sludge, to fertilize crops and add organic carbon to soil.

facts.text: By Swedish default values an adult excretes 0.55 kg nitrogen, 0.18 kg phosphorus and 0.36 kg potassium in feces a year, giving wet feces an NPK% of 1.1:0.8:0.9.
Post-treated dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets raise crop yields through their nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium and improve soil fertility through organic carbon.
Urine can hold up to 90% of the nitrogen, 50% of the phosphorus and 70% of the potassium in human excreta.
Fecal sludge from pit latrines, septic tanks and dry toilets can be made fit for farm use by dewatering, drying, composting, pelletizing or anaerobic digestion.

notes: Covers the Feces, Dried feces, Composted feces and Fecal sludge sections.

title: Biosolids

definition.text: Treated sewage sludge: solid organic matter recovered from sewage treatment and used as fertilizer or soil conditioner.

facts.text: Farmers began using sewage sludge in the 1920s, and research confirms biosolids hold nutrients similar to those in animal manures.
They can supply nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur and micronutrients, and are 60–65% organic matter that stimulates soil microbes.
Treated biosolids, in cake, granule, pellet or liquid form, are spread and worked into the soil or injected directly.
Biosolids can contain synthetic organic compounds, radionuclides and heavy metals; PFAS from spread biosolids has contaminated farm soils, groundwater, animals and crops.
Their use is controversial in some countries because of heavy metals and persistent pharmaceutical pollutants, and some places ban them on farmland.
Applying sewage sludge has been shown to raise soil available phosphorus and soil salinity.
One study found that high-temperature pyrolysis of biosolids into biochar reduced PFAS below detectable limits.
Treatment routes include anaerobic and aerobic digestion, composting, alkaline treatment that holds lime-mixed sludge above pH 12, heat drying and dewatering.

contested_note: Land application of sewage sludge is controversial in the USA and parts of Europe because of the pollutants it may carry.
