definition.text: The potential shortage of economically mineable phosphorus, a limited resource used up by fertilizer production.

facts.text: A shortage of mined phosphorus would threaten worldwide food security.
The term arose from the limited occurrence of rock phosphate; one estimate puts the US peak in 1988 and the world peak in 1989.
Phosphorus recovered from excreta, for example as struvite from urine or from sludge treatment liquids, is an alternative to mined phosphate ore.
Using less fertilizer, as when mycorrhizal inoculants allow lower rates, helps prolong finite phosphorus reserves.

conflicts.text: Peak phosphorus will occur within the next few hundred years, or perhaps earlier.
conflicts.note: Sustainable agriculture puts the world peak in the future; Soil fertility (S:2da45bb19b64) estimates it already occurred in 1989.

title: Multiple barrier approach
article: Reuse of human excreta#Multiple barrier concept for safe use in agriculture

definition.text: A series of treatment steps and other precautions that together prevent pathogens spreading when excreta are reused in farming.

facts.text: World Health Organization guidelines of 2006 on safe reuse of wastewater, excreta and greywater rest on this concept.
Barriers include choice of crop, farming and application methods and farmer education; how much treatment is needed depends on which other barriers are used.
Temperatures above 50 °C, as in thermophilic composting or digestion, or pH above 10, from ammonia or lime treatment, inactivate most pathogens.
Helminth eggs, among the hardest pathogens to destroy, serve as indicator organisms in reuse schemes.

title: Biofertilizer

definition.text: A substance containing living microorganisms that colonize the rhizosphere or plant interior and promote growth by increasing the supply or availability of nutrients.

facts.text: Biofertilizers add nutrients through nitrogen fixation and phosphorus solubilization and stimulate growth through growth-promoting substances.
Their microorganisms restore the soil's natural nutrient cycle and build soil organic matter.
Plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria and mycorrhizae increase nitrogen fixation, make inorganic phosphorus soluble, raise mineral bioavailability and produce hormones such as auxins and gibberellin.
They can reduce the use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides but cannot yet replace them.
Reported yield increases reach about 10–40%, through nitrogen fixation and higher protein, amino acid and vitamin content.
They also suppress plant pathogens, protect against drought and other stresses, and detoxify pollutants below ground.
Effects vary between and even within environments, and are most marked in drier climates.
Compost, compost tea and vermicompost-based inoculants are also used as biofertilizers.

conflicts.text: Biofertilizers increase crop yield by 20-30% and replace chemical nitrogen and phosphorus by 30%.
conflicts.note: Same Benefits section gives 'up to about 10–40%' in S:bf9a3af8e7f8; neither sentence states conditions.

notes: 2024 count of approved US products (S:dfe428bbe447) skipped as market detail.

definition.text: The organisms used in biofertilizers, longest among them the nitrogen fixers Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum and blue-green algae.

facts.text: Rhizobium inoculant is used for legumes, Azotobacter for crops such as wheat, maize, cotton and potato, and Azospirillum mainly for sorghum, millets, maize, sugarcane and wheat.
Nitrogen-fixing blue-green algae such as Nostoc and Anabaena inoculate paddy crops; Anabaena with the water fern Azolla can add up to 60 kg/ha of nitrogen per season.
Other organisms used include Bacillus and Bradyrhizobium bacteria, Trichoderma fungi and Gigaspora mycorrhizal fungi.
Seaweeds rich in potassium, phosphorus and trace elements are widely used in coastal districts in place of manure.

title: Biochar

definition.text: A form of charcoal, sometimes modified, made by heating biomass with little oxygen and intended for use in soil.

facts.text: It is the light, black residue of carbon and ash left after biomass is pyrolysed; it is sterile when made and gains life only after contact with soil organisms.
In soils it is used mainly to improve aeration and fertility, cut greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient leaching, reduce acidity and perhaps raise the water content of coarse soils.
Applied in excess, or made from a feedstock unsuited to the soil, it can harm soil organisms, reduce available water, alter pH and raise salinity.
Its refractory stability lets it persist in soils for thousands of years, the basis of biochar carbon removal.
Pre-Columbian Amazonians made it by smouldering farm waste under soil in pits or trenches, though whether they meant to improve the soil is unknown; settlers called the result terra preta.
The word is a late-20th-century coinage joining the Greek bios, life, with char.
Beyond soils it serves slash-and-char farming, animal feed, concrete mixes and water treatment, where it removes heavy metals, dyes and organic pollutants.

notes: S:d6a72f795415 (Etymology) is flagged CONTESTED, but it only reports online disagreement over whether biochar must be biologically active; not treated as a scholarly debate.

definition.text: Biochar is made mainly by pyrolysis, the heating of biomass without oxygen so that it decomposes instead of burning.

facts.text: Pyrolysis yields a solid (biochar), a liquid (bio-oil) and a gas (syngas); temperature, heating rate and residence time set the yield and can favour energy or char.
Gasifiers, which run through oxidation, drying, pyrolysis and reduction, make most biochar sold in the United States; their pyrolysis zone runs at 250–550 °C.

Smallholders make it without equipment by lighting crop-waste piles from the top and quenching the embers with soil or water, the top-down or conservation burn, which gives far less smoke than open burning.
Hydrothermal carbonization also yields a carbon-rich solid, but because the process differs the product is called hydrochar rather than biochar.

definition.text: The physical and chemical makeup of a biochar, set by its feedstock and production method, which explains how it performs in a given use.

facts.text: Properties are grouped by proximate and elemental composition, pH and porosity; the International Biochar Initiative publishes standard evaluation methods.
Hydrogen-to-carbon and oxygen-to-carbon ratios track polarity and aromaticity, and both fall during carbonization as hydrogen- and oxygen-bearing groups are driven off.
Pyrolysis at 450–550 °C leaves amorphous carbon; hotter runs progressively convert it into turbostratic graphene sheets.
Higher production temperatures raise conductivity, aromaticity and intrinsic recalcitrance, which governs how long the carbon lasts.

title: Biochar carbon removal

definition.text: Carbon sequestration by turning biomass into biochar, whose stable carbon then stays locked in soil or other materials.

facts.text: Making biochar releases CO2, up to 50% of the biomass, but the carbon that remains is stable and can stay in the ground for hundreds to thousands of years.
The World Bank says biochar keeps 10–70% (about 50% on average) of the original biomass carbon and slows its decomposition by one or two orders of magnitude.
Removal also counts when high-quality biochar goes into construction materials such as concrete and tar, not only into soils.
Charcoal-rich black spots in Belgian arable soils, left by kilns before 1870, showed lower respiration and slower carbon turnover.
Biochar can also store carbon indirectly by raising crop yields while possibly slowing carbon mineralization.
A 2021 review put potential removal at 1.6–3.2 billion tonnes of CO2 a year; economically feasible estimates are roughly 0.3–1.8 Gt CO2 a year at carbon prices below US$100 a tonne.
Actual deployment is small: production is on the order of a few hundred thousand tonnes a year, giving well under 1 Mt CO2 of certified removal annually.
A 2018 study doubted enough biomass exists for significant sequestration, and some authors warn that inflated expectations could bring a boom and bust.

contested_note: Sources disagree on how much carbon biochar can realistically remove: technical estimates reach billions of tonnes a year, while others doubt the biomass supply and warn of a boom and bust.

definition.text: Mixing biochar into or spreading it on soil to raise fertility, hold water and nutrients and store carbon over the medium to long term.

facts.text: Benefits are greatest in degraded tropical and nutrient-poor soils and smaller in temperate regions.
Its pores and high specific surface area make it hygroscopic, so it keeps water and dissolved nutrients in the upper soil and lowers fertilizer needs.
Modest additions cut nitrous oxide emissions by up to 80% and eliminate methane emissions.
It can reduce leaching of E. coli through sandy soils and remove heavy metals; soil biologist Elaine Ingham stressed its value as habitat for beneficial microbes.
Significant yield gains appear to need 2.5–20 tonnes per hectare, a cost often prohibitive for low-input field crops.
Its strong adsorption can reduce the effectiveness of pesticides, especially with high-surface-area biochars.
Effects depend on the biochar's properties, the dose, soil type and condition, temperature and humidity, and the mechanisms are still poorly understood.

definition.text: Adding calcium- and magnesium-rich materials such as marl, chalk, limestone, burnt lime or hydrated lime to soil.

facts.text: In acid soils these materials act as a base and neutralize acidity, often improving plant growth and soil bacterial activity, though oversupply can harm plants.
Most acid soils are saturated with aluminium rather than hydrogen ions, and their acidity generally comes from aluminium hydrolysis.
Sandy, heavily leached or strongly acid mineral soils are low in calcium and need liming, which can also offset the poor cation-exchange capacity that lets potassium leach.
Raising the pH by liming frequently relieves molybdenum deficiency by decreasing molybdenum sorption.
A German forestry study comparing stands two and twenty years after liming found it promoted nitrate leaching and lowered phosphorus in some leaves.
Modern liming was preceded by marling, the spreading of raw chalk and lime debris, with evidence dating to the 1200s in the British Isles.

definition.text: The amount of lime needed to neutralize an acid soil, which soil-testing laboratories work out from the soil's base saturation.

facts.text: How far a given dose raises pH depends on the soil's buffer capacity, which is generally related to its cation-exchange capacity.
Lime must neutralize the acid-forming ions held on soil colloids, not just those in the soil water, or they will restore the original pH.
Low-CEC soils show a sharper pH rise but lose the added bases faster to leaching, so they return to acidity sooner unless limed again.
Over-liming is most likely on low-CEC soils such as sands that lack organic matter and clay to buffer them.

definition.text: Liming aimed at improving aggregate stability in clay soils, usually with calcium oxide or hydroxide mixed with calcium carbonate.

facts.text: It can reduce losses of clay and nutrients from soil aggregates.
High calcium concentrations and ionic strength in the soil solution enhance flocculation of clay minerals, forming more stable aggregates.

definition.text: The net change in soil organic carbon after liming, the outcome of three processes pulling in different directions.

facts.text: Better growing conditions raise yields, returning more organic matter to the soil as dying roots and crop residue.
A more favourable pH briefly stimulates soil biological activity, speeding mineralization and turnover of organic matter.
Improved structure protects organic carbon from mineralization, as calcium-driven flocculation builds more stable aggregates.

definition.text: A soil additive of pulverized limestone or chalk whose main active component is calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Unlike quicklime and slaked lime, ground limestone needs no burning in a kiln, only milling; all these limes are used to supply a base that corrects acidity.
It raises the pH of acid soils, supplies calcium, improves water penetration and improves plant uptake of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
Lime is not a fertilizer, though it can be used together with fertilizers.
Soils become acid through leaching under high rainfall, removal of minerals by crops, and reactions of modern chemical fertilizers in the soil.
Dolomitic lime has similar effects while supplying magnesium as well as calcium.
A soil test is the best way to tell whether a soil is acidic or short of calcium or magnesium.
Fields were once usually limed with burnt lime, because affordable fine milling of stone only developed after the mid-19th century.
Other amendments that raise soil pH include wood ash, burnt lime, magnesium oxide, basic slag, silicate rock dust and oyster shells.

definition.text: A rating that compares a liming material's neutralizing power with that of pure calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Limestones containing dolomite can rate above 100 percent, because magnesium carbonate is lighter than calcium carbonate.
Soil acids are weak, so lime must be finely ground: particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and finer than 60 mesh fully effective.
The effective calcium carbonate equivalent (ECCE) combines CCE with fineness; commercial aglime typically ranges from 45 to 110 percent.
Marl application rates are adjusted for its lower calcium carbonate content using the calcium carbonate equivalent.

definition.text: The large-scale liming that turned Brazil's acidic, nutrient-poor cerrado into farmland from the 1960s on.

facts.text: Before the 1960s the inland cerrado was considered unfit for farming because its soil was too acidic and poor in nutrients.
Brazil spread 14–16 million tonnes of lime a year in the late 1990s, rising to 25 million tonnes in 2003 and 2004, about five tonnes per hectare.
The result helped make Brazil the world's second-biggest soybean exporter.

title: Aglime and strontium isotope studies
article: Agricultural lime#Effect on prehistoric mobility studies

definition.text: The distortion that agricultural lime introduces into strontium-based studies of where prehistoric people lived.

facts.text: The effect is significant in areas with calcium-poor soils.
In Denmark's Karup River catchment, more than half the strontium came from runoff of agricultural lime rather than the natural environment.
Comparing remains with lime-contaminated burial sites has led researchers to wrongly conclude that some prehistoric people came from far away.

definition.text: A material added to soil to improve its physical qualities, usually its fertility and sometimes its mechanics.

facts.text: Soil conditioners are usually seen as a subset of soil amendments, a broader category that also takes in many fertilizers and non-organic materials.
Examples include biochar, bone meal, compost, manure, straw, peat, vermiculite, sulfur, lime, water-absorbing polymers, biosolids and rock flour.
Their most common use is loosening soil that has become compacted, since compaction hampers root uptake of water and nutrients.
Many add nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus, and amendments can greatly raise cation-exchange capacity.
Organic material can greatly improve water retention in sandy soils, and conditioners can adjust pH for particular plants or make very acid or alkaline soils usable.
Soil testing should come before application to show which conditioner suits the soil.
Over-application can harm plants through excess salts, nitrogen and metals, and surplus nutrients can run off into waterways.
In construction, soil conditioning is also called soil stabilization.

definition.text: Synthetic polyacrylamide polymers added to soil to improve its structure and how it handles water.

facts.text: Introduced in the 1950s as linear soil conditioners, they were presented at a 1951 symposium on improving soil structure.
Water-soluble forms increase pore space and infiltration in clay soils, make soil friable and let it dry and be worked sooner after rain.
Cross-linked forms hold water strongly and are used in horticulture, agriculture and some potting soils.
On construction sites they are used for erosion control to protect the water quality of nearby streams.

definition.text: Polymers such as polyacrylamides and polymethacrylates that absorb several hundred times their own weight in water, tested as soil conditioners.

facts.text: The first synthetic soil conditioners appeared in the 1950s, chiefly hydrolysed polyacrylonitrile.
Trials in agriculture, horticulture and landscaping from the 1960s stalled when the polymers proved phytotoxic from residual acrylamide monomer.
Even after monomer levels fell below toxic levels, few studies show these polymers improving plant quality or survival.
Such materials are judged on cost-effectiveness, how long they raise soil moisture, and their effects on microbes, nutrient levels and plant survival.

definition.text: A layer of material applied to the surface of soil.

facts.text: It is used to conserve soil moisture, improve soil fertility and health, suppress weeds, regulate soil temperature and improve appearance.
Mulch is usually organic but not always; it may be permanent, like plastic sheeting, or temporary, like bark chips.
Layers are normally 5 centimetres (2 in) or more deep.
Early in the season mulch warms soil by keeping heat otherwise lost at night, allowing earlier sowing; later it stabilizes soil temperature and moisture.
It cuts evaporation, but can also intercept light rain, and overly thick layers can reduce oxygen in the soil.
Mulches of manure and compost are worked into the soil naturally by worms and other organisms.
Mulch is also laid to prevent soil erosion on slopes.
Materials are chosen for availability, cost, appearance, effect on soil chemistry and pH, durability, decomposition rate and freedom from weed seeds and pathogens.

definition.text: Mulch of plant or animal residues, such as leaves, straw, bark, wood chips or manure, which decays over time.

facts.text: Straw, peat, sawdust and wood products can briefly slow plant growth because their wide carbon-to-nitrogen ratio lets decomposing microbes draw nitrogen from the soil.
Organic mulches can mat into a barrier to water and air, and vertically applied ones can wick water up and dry the soil.
Fully composted material is used to avoid phytotoxicity, and seed-free material to avoid bringing in weeds.
Peat moss can form a crust that water cannot soak into once wetted and dried, and it lowers surface pH, suiting acid-loving plants.

definition.text: Thin plastic sheeting laid over soil, with crops growing through slits or holes in it.

facts.text: It dominates large-scale vegetable growing, covering millions of acres worldwide each year.
Because it is impermeable, drip tape is usually laid underneath; black and clear films capture sunlight and warm the soil.
Polyethylene mulch must be removed at the end of the season, or it breaks into fragments that pollute the soil with ketones and aldehydes.
Biodegradable films of plant starches or sugars are broken down by soil microorganisms into water and carbon dioxide and can be tilled in.

definition.text: Low groundcover plants grown under a main crop to slow weeds and give the other benefits of mulch.

facts.text: They are usually fast-growing plants that keep growing with the crop, whereas cover crops are worked into the soil or killed.
They may eventually need to be killed mechanically or chemically to stop them competing with the main crop.
Clovers can fix nitrogen, and creeping comfrey can gather nutrients from the subsoil.

definition.text: Organic mulch that has turned anaerobic and smells of vinegar, ammonia, sulfur or silage.

facts.text: It develops when nitrogen-rich material is not turned often enough and forms pockets of intense decomposition.
The anaerobic process makes small amounts of phytotoxic compounds, which can linger for a while after the material is aerated again.
Low-growing and newly planted plants suffer most, and some seeds may fail to germinate.

definition.text: A salt of ammonium and nitrate ions that is an important nitrogen fertilizer, with an NPK rating of 34-0-0.

facts.text: It is less concentrated than urea (46-0-0) but more stable, and does not rapidly lose nitrogen to the atmosphere.
It is made by reacting ammonia from the Haber process with nitric acid.
Natural deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert were mined until the Haber–Bosch process made nitrate mining obsolete.
It forms explosive mixtures with fuels, so it is a greater security risk than urea, which is not an oxidizer.

title: Perlite

definition.text: An amorphous volcanic glass, usually formed by hydration of obsidian, that expands greatly when heated.

facts.text: At 850–900 °C its trapped water vaporizes, expanding it to 7–16 times its original volume as a brilliant white material.
As a soil amendment it is highly permeable, holds little water and helps prevent compaction; alone it serves for hydroponics and rooting cuttings.
In potting mixes perlite and vermiculite improve aeration and water retention, and cacti and succulents need a large share of perlite or sand for drainage.

notes: Perlite page (S:4b897e6b0d11) says it has low water retention; Potting soil (S:4f6a67ddbbbe) says perlite and vermiculite improve water retention. Different contexts, not the same quantity; flagged for the verification pass.

definition.text: Any liquid that passes through a material and carries away dissolved or suspended components of it.

facts.text: In environmental science the term means a liquid carrying harmful substances that can enter the environment, most often from landfills.
Composting sites produce leachate in wet periods, as rain makes decomposed matter flow off as runoff.
Stockpiled coal and mine wastes yield leachate when sulfide minerals exposed to air form sulfuric acid, often rich in metals.
Acidic leachate flushed from acid sulfate soils can harm groundwater and surface waters, with effects that may persist or peak after dry spells.

definition.text: Contaminated liquid formed when rain or other water percolates through landfill waste, which can pollute groundwater if not managed.

facts.text: Its composition varies with the landfill's age and waste type; it carries dissolved and suspended matter, and decomposition adds organic acids, aldehydes, alcohols and simple sugars.
Risks are cut by siting landfills on impermeable ground or lining them with geomembranes or engineered clay; bentonite is used to line landfill bases.
In a 2012 New York survey, all double-lined landfill cells leaked less than 500 litres per hectare per day.
Granular laterite in constructed wetlands has removed phosphorus and heavy metals from landfill leachate.

definition.text: Fine, silt-sized rock particles made by glaciers grinding bedrock, or by artificial grinding to a similar size.

facts.text: Although clay-sized, the particles are ground quartz and feldspar rather than clay minerals; carried far by wind they form loess.
As rock dust it is used in organic farming as a soil conditioner supplying micronutrients; basalt and granite are richest, while limestone is often deficient.
A 2022 study found basalt dust raised available phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium within months; in forests rock flour slowly raises soil pH and buffering.
Nutrient-poor soils may need 10 to 50 tonnes per hectare; the German miller Julius Hensel reported success with stonemeal in the 1890s.

title: Carbon farming

definition.text: A set of farming methods that aim to store carbon in soil and biomass, for a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere.

facts.text: Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using organic mulch or compost, working with biochar and terra preta, and changing crop types; forestry adds reforestation and bamboo.
Converting forest, grassland or savanna to cropland cuts soil organic carbon by about 30–40%, largely because harvests remove carbon-bearing plant material.
The loss can be countered by adding carbon, for example by leaving harvest residues, applying manure or rotating perennial crops with their larger root biomass.
More soil organic matter aids plant growth, improves water retention and reduces fertilizer use.
Gains are reversible: disturbance or intensive tillage turns soil into a greenhouse gas source, and after several decades soils saturate and stop absorbing carbon.
Plowing splits aggregates so microbes consume their organic compounds, briefly lifting yield before the lost structure reduces water holding and erosion resistance.
It costs more than conventional farming, US$3–130 per tonne of CO2 sequestered depending on region, and some countries subsidize it.
By 2016 carbon farming variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares of the nearly 5 billion hectares of world farmland.

contested_note: Many researchers dispute the soil-carbon benefits claimed for managed grazing, and the effect of added soil carbon on yields is not settled.

title: Compost for soil carbon
article: Carbon farming#Using organic mulch and compost

definition.text: Spreading compost over the soil surface without tilling so that it stores carbon in a stable form.

facts.text: A 2013 study found a single compost application significantly and durably raised grassland carbon storage by 25–70%.
Forage output rose 78% at a drier valley site and 42% at a wetter coastal site, with no significant rise in methane or nitrous oxide emissions.
Composting is not an NRCS-approved technique, and commercial compost supplies are too limited to cover large areas.

title: Grazing management and soil carbon

definition.text: The dispute over whether rotating livestock through small paddocks builds carbon in grassland soils.

facts.text: Rotating herds lets paddocks rest and favours deep-rooted perennials over shallow-rooted annual grasses that die once grazed.
Only a small amount of carbon may be stored in grassland soils through root exudates and manure, while ruminants also emit methane.
Many researchers argue the approach cannot deliver the benefits claimed, and studies find that excluding livestock from semi-arid grasslands can recover vegetation and soil carbon.

contested_note: Advocates credit rotational grazing with building soil carbon, but many researchers dispute the claimed benefits and find livestock exclusion can do more.

definition.text: An earthy material rich in carbonate minerals, clay and silt, which becomes marlstone when hardened into rock.

facts.text: Marls typically contain 35–65% clay and 65–35% carbonate, mostly calcite.
It forms in marine or fresh water, often through algae; marl lakes in recently glaciated areas and very rich fens deposit it from calcium-rich water.
It is used as a soil conditioner and to neutralize acid soil, adding calcium, improving structure and making other nutrients more available.
Because its carbonate is mostly calcium carbonate, marled crops may show magnesium deficiency unless magnesium is also supplied.

definition.text: Spreading marl, or raw chalk and lime debris, on fields to improve the soil, one of the oldest soil amendments in agriculture.

facts.text: Marl was used sporadically in Britain from prehistoric times, and Pliny the Elder mentioned its use in the 1st century.
Wider use from the 16th century contributed to the early modern agricultural revolution; in 18th-century Lancashire almost every field had its marl pit.
Lime and imported mineral fertilizers gradually replaced marl early in the 19th century.
By the late 19th century New Jersey mined marl industrially, grading it and publishing detailed chemical analyses.

title: Seaweed fertiliser

definition.text: Organic fertilizer made from seaweed and used to raise soil fertility and plant growth.

facts.text: Brown seaweeds are used most; seaweed may be laid as mulch, composted, dried and powdered, or made into liquid extracts.
It supplies macro- and micronutrients, humic acids and plant hormones, and can raise crop tolerance of low moisture, high salinity and freezing.
As a soil conditioner its humic acid and soluble alginates help clay soils short of organic matter gain better texture, aeration and water retention.
Heavy metals accumulated by seaweed may pass into crops, one of several challenges alongside the spread of diseases and invasive species.

notes: S:810e93fcbb76 says the compounds make clay particles aggregate 'by stimulating clay disaggregation', which contradicts itself; worth checking in verification.

definition.text: Damage to a plant caused by too much fertilizer, the wrong type of fertilizer, or too little water applied with it.

facts.text: Excess salt, nitrogen or ammonia impairs photosynthesis and respiration, causing visible burns.
When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots, so the plant responds as in drought.
Early signs are white salt marks and crusts around the roots; later the leaves brown and die, root growth stops and roots may rot.
Dry, overheated plants are most susceptible; salt burns are treated by heavy watering to wash the salts away, or by cleaning the roots and repotting.

definition.text: A measure of how much a fertilizer raises the osmotic pressure of water, compared with sodium nitrate set at 100.

facts.text: Fertilizers with a salt index above 20 are not recommended for particularly sensitive crops.
Potassium chloride has a salt index of 116.2, urea 74.4 and diammonium phosphate 29.2.
Using too much fertilizer, or one with too high a salt index, builds up salts in the soil and causes burns.

definition.text: The loss of fertilizer nitrogen to the air as ammonia gas when urea breaks down at the soil surface.

facts.text: The enzyme urease hydrolyses urea to unstable carbamic acid, which breaks down without enzymes into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
The ammonia escapes unless it reacts with water to form ammonium, which plants can use and ammonia cannot.
The reaction makes hydroxide, raising pH near each urea particle to around 9.0, which increases volatilization and makes the zone toxic for several hours.
Without enough moisture, up to thirty percent of the available nitrogen can be lost to the air within seventy-two hours of application.
Losses rise with temperature, pH and drying soil; urea hydrolysed completely within two days on soils of pH about 8.2 or more but took twice as long at pH 5.2.
Surface residues and organic-rich soils carry more urease and so lose more, while about 0.1 inch of rain soon after application moves urea into the soil.
Incorporating or injecting urea reduces losses, because good soil contact buffers pH and slows ammonia formation.
Urea makes up more than fifty percent of the world's nitrogen fertilizers, so these losses matter for yields and costs.

title: Urease inhibitors

definition.text: Additives that block the urease enzyme so that urea fertilizer stays in its non-volatile form for longer.

facts.text: Most studies find they reduce nitrogen losses when fertilizer must be applied in poor field conditions.
They give rain time to carry urea into the soil, so hydrolysis happens below the surface and less nitrogen escapes.
They also shrink the zones of high pH around untreated urea, and help most in high-residue conservation tillage.
NBPT, a common inhibitor sold as an enhanced efficiency fertilizer, is mixed with urea at about 0.5% by weight.

conflicts.text: Urease inhibitors are added to urea-based fertilizers at 0.05 weight percent.
conflicts.note: Tenfold below the NBPT page's 0.5% by weight; one figure may be a slip.

notes: The page N-(n-Butyl)thiophosphoric triamide is folded in here rather than given a product entry.

definition.text: Gardening in soil raised above ground level and usually enclosed in a frame.

facts.text: The soil is usually enriched with compost, and crops are planted so close that their touching leaves suppress weeds and conserve moisture.
Because no one walks on the beds, the soil is not compacted and roots grow easily; beds also extend the season and avoid poor native soil.
Built along contour lines on slopes, they help control erosion and conserve water and nutrients.
Gardeners on heavy red clay Ultisols use raised beds or Hügelkultur to avoid amending the soil.

title: Slash-and-char

definition.text: An alternative to slash-and-burn in which cleared vegetation is charred instead of burned, leaving biochar for the soil.

facts.text: Slash-and-burn leaves only 3% of the organic carbon in the soil, whereas slash-and-char can keep up to 50% in a highly stable form.
Shifting from slash-and-burn to slash-and-char could sequester an estimated 0.22–0.42 Gt of carbon a year.
Slash-and-burn soils soon lose their nutrients and are abandoned, whereas biochar-enriched soils can sustain cropping indefinitely.
The char, mixed with crop residues, food waste or manure and buried, can form terra preta, itself a product of Amazonian slash-and-char farming.

conflicts.text: Replacing slash-and-burn with slash-and-char could offset up to 12% of land-use-change emissions, 0.21 gigatonnes a year.
conflicts.note: Carbon farming gives 0.21 Gt a year for the same switch; Biochar (S:d4c306ef5023) gives 0.22–0.42 Gt C a year.

notes: The Slash-and-char lead calls terra preta the only soil known to regenerate itself (S:db06e1b98ec3, CITATION NEEDED); not used.

title: Hügelkultur

definition.text: A horticultural technique in which a mound of decaying wood and other compostable plant matter is planted as a raised bed.

facts.text: Advocates claim it improves fertility, water retention and soil warming; the term was first published in a 1962 German gardening booklet by Herrman Andrä.
Wood has one of the highest carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, so its decay may tie up soil nitrogen at first, lowering fertility for perhaps one to two years.
Peer-reviewed studies are few; a student thesis found hügel mounds held almost twice as much water as flat control plots.
Critics say it lacks genuine scientific principles and runs counter to soil building by litterfall, since in nature wood decays at the surface.

contested_note: Permaculture advocates promote it on personal experience, while critics say it lacks a scientific basis and peer-reviewed evidence is scarce.

definition.text: A liquid fertilizer made of urea and ammonium nitrate dissolved in water.

facts.text: The mixture has a very low critical relative humidity (18% at 30 °C), so it can only be used as a liquid.
Together the two salts are far more soluble than either alone, giving a stable solution with 32% total nitrogen.
The commonest grade, UAN 32, is 45% ammonium nitrate, 35% urea and only 20% water; UAN 28, UAN 30 and UAN 18 also exist.
The solutions corrode mild steel, and mixed with calcium nitrate solutions they form a precipitate that can plug nozzles.

definition.text: Ground animal bones and slaughterhouse waste, used as a livestock supplement and as a slow-release organic fertilizer.

facts.text: It supplies phosphorus and calcium with little nitrogen; its N-P-K rating is typically 3–15–0, with about 12% calcium.
Being insoluble in water, it must be broken down by soil acidity or microbial acids, releasing nutrients only in acidic soils (pH < 7.0) over 1 to 4 months.
Liebig suggested dissolving bones in sulphuric acid around 1840, and the process was first used in Britain in 1841.
Before that, farmers on nutrient-depleted soils crushed bones collected from battlefields such as Waterloo and Austerlitz.

definition.text: An organic compound derived from urea (IBDU) that acts as a controlled-release nitrogen fertilizer.

facts.text: Unlike urea, IBDU is not water-soluble, and its low solubility limits how fast it hydrolyses to fast-acting urea.
It is made by condensing isobutyraldehyde with two equivalents of urea, and releases nitrogen by the reverse reaction once dissolved.
Related urea-based slow-release materials include crotonylidene diurea and urea-formaldehyde products such as ureaform.

definition.text: Feeding plants by applying liquid fertilizer directly to their leaves.

facts.text: Leaves absorb nutrients through their stomata and epidermis.
In the 1950s H. B. Tukey and S. H. Wittwer at Michigan State traced radioactive phosphorus and potassium sprayed on leaves moving about one foot per hour through the plant.
It avoids leaching losses and helps most with phosphorus, zinc and iron, which soils fix or hold in poorly available forms.
It is best done in early morning or late evening below 24 °C (75 °F), since heat closes leaf pores in some species.

title: Milorganite

definition.text: A brand of heat-dried biosolids fertilizer made by treating Milwaukee's sewage sludge.

facts.text: Heat-dried biosolids contain slow-release organic nitrogen, mostly insoluble phosphorus bound with iron and aluminium, and much organic matter.
Biosolids can carry synthetic organic compounds, radionuclides and heavy metals, and US limits cover metals including arsenic, cadmium, copper, lead and mercury.
Its name, from Milwaukee Organic Nitrogen, won a 1925 naming contest.

notes: A product brand, excluded per the guide even though it has its own article; the soil-relevant content (heat-dried biosolids) belongs with the sewage sludge / biosolids material in Reuse of human excreta.

definition.text: A chemical phosphate fertilizer made by treating phosphate-rich material, first bones and later phosphate rock, with acid.

facts.text: First made in the 1840s from bones and sulfuric acid, it was then made from phosphate coprolites and later from phosphorite.
John Bennet Lawes patented his 'super phosphate of lime' and in 1842 began making it from fossil coprolites on an industrial scale, the world's first chemical manure.
Much of its phosphate is soluble and immediately available, giving plants a quick boost, and it is relatively cheap, so it is widely used in developing regions.
In soil, phosphate readily binds to clays, aluminium and iron salts or organic ligands, becoming largely unavailable to plants.
Single superphosphate comes from phosphate rock and sulfuric acid; triple superphosphate, mainly monocalcium phosphate, from rock and phosphoric acid; double superphosphate mixes both.
Typical fertilizer-grade triple superphosphate contains 45% P2O5 equivalent and single superphosphate 20%.
Continuous use can acidify soils, especially poorly buffered ones.
Its soluble phosphate, and phosphate bound to fine sediments, washes into rivers, where it is lost to farming and feeds eutrophication.

conflicts.note: Fertilizer page gives 14–18% for single superphosphate; Superphosphate page gives a typical 20% P2O5 equivalent.

title: Phosphorite

definition.text: Phosphate rock: a non-detrital sedimentary rock rich in phosphate minerals.

facts.text: Its grade ranges from 4% to 20% P2O5, against under 0.2% phosphorus in average sedimentary rock.
Fertilizer industry rock must be beneficiated, by washing, flotation and similar steps, to at least 28% P2O5, and most marketed grades reach 30% or more.
The phosphate is mostly fluorapatite in very fine masses, with hydroxyapatite often derived from bones and teeth.
Phosphorites form mostly in shallow marine settings, most commonly where strong upwelling brings deep phosphate-rich water to the coast.
About 90% of rock phosphate goes to fertilizer and animal feed supplements.
Mined rock is made into wet-process phosphoric acid, which with more rock gives triple superphosphate, or with ammonia gives ammonium phosphates.
World economic reserves were 70 gigatonnes in 2018, but high-grade ore is declining.
Beneficiated rock is sold as an 'organic' phosphate source, and an FAO report finds direct application can be more sustainable in certain soils and countries.

notes: Farming systems has Rock phosphate fertilizer on Agrogeology#Rock phosphate as fertilizer (direct application); this entry is the rock and ore itself.

definition.text: The material left after anaerobic digestion of a biodegradable feedstock, the other main product besides biogas.

facts.text: Feedstocks include sewage sludge, livestock manure, energy crops such as maize, food and municipal waste, crop residues and industrial wastes, and they set its chemistry.
Acidogenic digestate is fibrous solid matter rich in lignin and cellulose that holds moisture well.
Methanogenic digestate is a liquid sludge high in ammonium and potassium.
The liquid fraction is up to 90% of the volume, with 2–6% dry matter and most soluble N and K; the solid fraction keeps most of the phosphorus.
Ammonia is usually 60–80% of its total nitrogen, up to 99% from kitchen food waste, and it carries more phosphorus and potassium than compost.
Its main use is as a soil conditioner: the solid part adds organic matter and water retention, the liquid part nutrients, and it can protect soil from erosion.
It is not technically compost, which forms aerobically and breaks down lignin and cellulose further.
Quality is judged on heavy metals, nutrients, pathogens and physical contaminants; in the UK, digestate meeting PAS110 ceases to be waste and can be sold as bio-fertiliser.

definition.text: Magnesium ammonium phosphate, a phosphate mineral with formula NH4MgPO4·6H2O.

facts.text: It forms in alkaline conditions from equal molar amounts of magnesium, ammonium and phosphate, and dissolves readily in acid but only sparingly in neutral or alkaline water.
It scales pipes and pumps in wastewater plants, especially after anaerobic digesters release ammonium and phosphate.
Recovering phosphorus from manure and municipal wastewater as struvite for fertilizer appears promising.
First described as a fertilizer in 1857, it supplies phosphorus, nitrogen and magnesium, and can be made from urine by raising pH and adding magnesium.

definition.text: The capture, storage, treatment and use of animal manure in an environmentally sustainable way.

facts.text: Manure can be liquid, slurry or solid, and includes bedding and urine as well as feces.
A part of nutrient management, it aims to spread manure on fields in amounts that enrich soil without polluting water.
Stored manure gives off hydrogen sulfide, methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide, peaking when it is agitated for pumping; in confined spaces the gases can kill.
Hydrogen sulfide deadens smell at about 100 to 150 ppm, and 500 to 700 ppm can kill within 30 to 60 minutes.
About 33% of global ammonia emissions in 2018 could be attributed to manure.
Over-application can acidify soil and build up heavy metals, together reducing fertility.
Runoff and leaching carry nutrients, pathogens, antibiotics, hormones and heavy metals from manured fields to water, driving eutrophication.
Mitigating practices include anaerobic digestion to biogas and digestate, composting, separating solids from liquids, and vegetated buffer strips.

definition.text: Controlled-release fertilizers made of urea prills coated in less-soluble materials such as sulfur or polymers.

facts.text: The coatings release urea gradually, lowering the risk of fertilizer burn and allowing less frequent applications.
Sulfur-coated urea, 32% to 41% nitrogen and developed by the Tennessee Valley Authority, releases once water enters cracks in the coating; a wax seal slows it further until microbes degrade it.
Polymer-coated urea releases nitrogen more precisely, with release delayable for 10 months, but costs more than sulfur-coated urea.
Combination products coat urea with sulfur and then polymer, a cheaper route to precise release.

title: Bokashi

definition.text: An anaerobic, fermentation-based composting method that turns food waste and other organic matter into a soil amendment using specialized bran.

facts.text: Waste inoculated with yeast, photosynthetic bacteria and lactic acid bacteria ferments for a few weeks in an airtight vessel and is preserved by lactic acid, much like silage.
Mixed into soil, the lactate-rich preserve is eaten by soil life, mainly bacteria, within a few weeks, and earthworm action gives the soil a vermicompost-like texture.
Unlike aerobic compost it barely heats, loses little carbon as carbon dioxide and almost no nitrogen as nitrous oxide or ammonia, and lowers the risk of nutrient leaching.
It began in Korea; Teruo Higa's commercial 'EM' (Effective Microorganisms) method of 1982 became the best known form.

contested_note: Nobody disputes that EM starts the fermentation, but other claims, such as direct soil inoculation and whether benefits come from particular microbes, are robustly contested.

definition.text: A genus of seven small floating aquatic ferns, the mosquito ferns, that host a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium.

facts.text: Its partner, the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae, fixes atmospheric nitrogen and passes directly from one plant generation to the next.
It can double its biomass in 1.9 days and yield 8–10 tonnes of fresh matter per hectare in Asian paddy fields.
Planted in flooded rice paddies, it covers the water and suppresses weeds, then releases nitrogen to the rice as it dies; it is widely used as a biofertilizer in southeast Asia.
Rice farmers used it as a biofertilizer 1500 years ago; the earliest known written record is Jia Sixie's Qimin Yaoshu of 554 CE.

definition.text: A substance, microbial culture or mixture used to promote crop growth that is neither a pesticide nor a fertilizer.

facts.text: A proposed standard definition calls it a biological product that improves productivity through emergent properties of its constituents, not merely through known nutrients, growth regulators or protective compounds.

Recognised constituents include humic substances, amino acids, inorganic salts, seaweed extracts and chitin derivatives; biological agents include growth-promoting rhizobacteria, non-pathogenic fungi and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.
Endophytic biostimulants from registered microbial strains have improved nutrient use efficiency and abiotic stress tolerance under field conditions.
With no agreed definition, as of 2016 no country had a specific regulatory framework for them; some treat them under fertilizer law.

definition.text: A water-soluble ammonium phosphate salt, (NH4)2HPO4, made by reacting ammonia with phosphoric acid and used as fertilizer.

facts.text: Its typical NPK rating is 18-46-0: 18% nitrogen, 46% P2O5 and no K2O.
It raises soil pH at first, but over the long term the ground becomes more acidic than before as its ammonium is nitrified.
Its solution averages pH 7.5–8, and it is incompatible with alkaline chemicals, which turn its ammonium into ammonia.
It slowly loses ammonia in air and breaks down to ammonia and monoammonium phosphate at around 70 °C.

title: Ecological sanitation

definition.text: An approach to sanitation that aims to reuse human excreta safely in agriculture, closing the nutrient loop between sanitation and farming.

facts.text: It is an approach rather than a technology; urine-diverting dry toilets are its most common technology but not the only one.
Agricultural trials around the world show measurable benefits from treated excreta, especially urine, as fertilizer and soil conditioner.
It also answers a possible phosphorus shortage: one review suggested phosphate collected from urine could meet 22% of total demand.
How well its treatments destroy pathogens is still debated, though WHO reuse guidelines with a multiple barrier concept give a common framework.

contested_note: Proponents and opponents continue to debate whether ecosan treatment processes destroy pathogens safely.

definition.text: The accumulated excrement of seabirds or bats, used as fertilizer.

facts.text: It is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium; seabird and bat guano both exceed 40% organic matter, and bat guano may hold up to 6% available P2O5.
The word comes from Quechua, and Andean people may have used seabird guano from Peru's coastal islands as a soil amendment for as long as 5,000 years.
After Alexander von Humboldt studied it in 1802 and Humphry Davy praised Peruvian guano, it became popular in Europe in the 19th century.
The 19th-century seabird guano trade played a pivotal role in the rise of modern input-intensive farming.
European guano was poorer because high rainfall and humidity leached its potency.
Demand fell rapidly after 1910 with the Haber–Bosch process, but organic food has revived it in the 21st century.
Unsustainable seabird guano mining has destroyed habitat and killed millions of seabirds, and harvesting bat guano can drive bats from their roosts.

definition.text: The 19th-century era of large-scale guano export, from Humboldt's investigations at Callao in 1802 to the War of the Pacific.

facts.text: From 1840 Peru made guano an exclusive state resource, and its royalties became the country's largest source of revenue.
By 1846, 462,057 tonnes had been shipped from Ichaboe Island off Namibia to Britain; the biggest markets in 1840–1879 were Britain, the Low Countries, Germany and the United States.
Peru's exports peaked above 700,000 tonnes in 1870 despite the near exhaustion of the Chincha Islands; afterwards Chile saltpetre eclipsed guano.
The US Guano Islands Act of 1856 let citizens claim unclaimed islands holding guano, and nearly 100 islands were annexed.

definition.text: A mixture of animal waste and organic matter, sometimes thinned with water, used as farm fertilizer.

facts.text: It can be aged in a slurry pit to concentrate it, and it was developed in the 20th century as an alternative to fermented manure.
Like solid manure it is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium that come from the animals' feed.
Powerful post-war tractors could haul heavy tanks, letting farmers spread liquid manure evenly near plant roots.

Concentrated animal feeding operations supply most liquid manure spread on US vegetable fields, a route for E. coli O157:H7; runoff from such operations contaminated wells in the fatal Walkerton outbreak.

title: Nutrient budgeting

definition.text: A comparison of all the nutrients applied to a farm's soil with all those removed from the land.

facts.text: Inputs include fertilizer, rainfall, brought-in supplements and spread effluent; outputs include sold stock, crops and products such as milk, meat and wool, plus nitrate leaching, volatilization and phosphate runoff.
A surplus, with inputs above outputs, builds up nutrients and the risk of loss; a deficit depletes reserves and risks deficiencies and lower yields.

Less exact than a financial statement, a budget draws on yield history, past applications, average removal coefficients and nutrients in irrigation water, and is a best management practice in the 4R strategy.
In turf, sensors and variable-rate application put fertilizer only where uptake potential is highest, shrinking the surplus and leaching into urban watersheds.

notes: Extends existing entry with Building Soils 19.3.

title: Phosphogypsum

definition.text: The calcium sulfate hydrate, mainly gypsum, left as a by-product when phosphoric acid for fertilizer is made from phosphate rock.

facts.text: About five tons form per ton of phosphoric acid, an estimated 100 to 280 million tonnes a year worldwide.
Uranium at 5–10 ppm, thorium and their daughter nuclides make it weakly radioactive, so most is stored indefinitely; up to 15% of production is used, partly as a soil amendment.
In 1990 the US EPA banned most uses of phosphogypsum with more than 10 picocuries of radium-226 per gram.
It can pollute through phosphorus that drives eutrophication, toxic heavy metals and radioactivity, and its contents leach into groundwater and soil.

contested_note: Long-term storage of phosphogypsum is called controversial, and the EPA approved its use in roads in 2020 over environmentalists' objections, then withdrew the rule in 2021.
notes: Contested note draws on S:f0e7dafe6323, S:a7a36174b67d, S:6c777fdbefc7, S:2544126286bf.

definition.text: An evaporite mineral, a hydrated sulfate of potassium, calcium and magnesium, used as fertilizer.

facts.text: It supplies four nutrients and is low in chloride: 48% SO3, 14% K2O, 6% MgO and 17% CaO.
As a soil amendment it can improve drainage and fertility and help reduce soil acidity.
The only polyhalite mined comes from a 260-million-year-old layer more than 1,000 m below North Yorkshire, worked at Boulby Mine since 2010.

definition.text: The powdery residue left when wood burns, made up largely of calcium compounds.

facts.text: As a fertilizer it supplies potassium and calcium carbonate, which acts as a liming agent to neutralise acid soils.
It typically holds 7–33% calcium, 3–10% potassium, 1–2% magnesium and 0.3–1.4% phosphorus; calcium carbonate may be 25% or even 45% of its weight.
Burning wood leaves about 6–10% ash on average; hotter fires leave less and drive off potassium, sulfur and boron.
It also carries trace heavy metals, such as lead at 2–500 ppm and cadmium at 0.18–60 ppm.

title: Converting NPK labels to elemental content
article: Labeling of fertilizer#Converting nutrient analysis to composition

definition.text: Calculating a fertilizer's elemental phosphorus and potassium from the P2O5 and K2O values on its NPK label.

facts.text: P2O5 is 43.6% phosphorus by weight, so elemental phosphorus is 0.436 times the P value; K2O is 83% potassium, so elemental potassium is 0.83 times the K value.
The N value already gives elemental nitrogen by weight and needs no conversion.
An 18-51-20 fertilizer thus holds 18% nitrogen, 22% phosphorus and 17% potassium.
Pure potassium chloride, 52% potassium, would be labelled 0-0-63; sylvite, which contains other compounds, is usually labelled 0-0-60.

title: Fertilizer placement

definition.text: Where fertilizer is put relative to the crop, such as broadcast over the field or banded with the seed, a choice that can strongly affect how efficiently crops take it up.

facts.text: Broadcast applications of urea beyond what plants use cause nitrous oxide emissions and water pollution.
Because hydrolysing urea creates a toxic high-ammonia zone, urea fertilizers should not be applied or banded with seed at more than 10–20 kg/ha, depending on the crop.
Fertigation places nutrients wherever the irrigation water goes.

notes: Phrase-dossier concept with no page; the dossier's 'banding' hits were almost all off-topic, so facts come from search.

definition.text: Specialized crop-only and animal-only farms break the nutrient cycle, causing nutrient excess on one and depletion on the other.

facts.text: Animal operations such as CAFOs often import feed from afar, so supplying crop farms need large fertilizer amounts to replace the exported nutrients.
Manure piling up relative to the land base can be applied beyond crop needs, polluting ground and surface water, and stored manure can contaminate surface water directly.
Animals excrete most of the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in their feed, so animal-product farms export few nutrients, whereas annual grain and vegetable farms export many.

Annual-only farms have little reason to grow perennial forages; growing only one or two annuals complicates weed control, forgoes multi-year grass and legume soil health, favours pests and demands much nitrogen fertilizer.
Integrating livestock can make a farm more sustainable but more complex, and done wrongly can add environmental problems.

definition.text: Integrated crop-livestock farms grow all or nearly all of their animal feed and come in two general types.

facts.text: One type mainly sells animal products and matches animal numbers to the land's carrying capacity, such as grass-fed beef, pastured hogs or dairy growing its own grain and forage.
The other is the diversified farm that raises all its feed but sells a range of crops and animal products.
Multiple products protect against seasonal failure and price swings.
Crops feed animals and manure returns to the soil, giving a continuous supply of organic materials; perennial forages cut erosion and keep or raise soil organic matter.

definition.text: Farm manure has considerable economic value as a source of nutrients and soil organic matter.

facts.text: After cheap fertilizer arrived post-war, manure came to be seen as waste to dispose of; it is better spread widely than concentrated in a few places.
U.S. manure from 100 million cattle, 120 million hogs and 9 billion chickens holds about 23 million tons of nitrogen.

Nutrients in manure from a 100-cow dairy may exceed $20,000 a year, a 100-sow farrow-to-finish operation about $16,000, a 20,000-bird broiler operation about $6,000; soil organic matter benefits may double the value.

definition.text: The type of barn on a dairy farm frequently determines how manure is handled, as solid, semi-solid or liquid.

facts.text: Dairy manure with bedding at around 20% dry matter or more is spread as solid; liquid manure from free-stall barns is 2-12% dry matter; 12-20% is semi-solid, as with pasture cow manure.

Composting stabilizes nutrients, though considerable ammonium is lost, and gives less, more pleasant material to spread; separating liquid from solids lets solids compost without added material and eases transport.
Compost barns stir the bedded pack twice daily to 8-10 inches and clear it in spring or fall; vermicomposting uses worms to turn dairy manure into castings.
Industrial hog farms use slatted floors over pits and hold liquid manure in ponds for spring and fall spreading; small hoop-house hog systems use bedding.

definition.text: Storing manure lets farmers apply it at the best time for the crop, cutting runoff, leaching and gaseous losses, but storage itself loses nutrients.

facts.text: In one study, dairy manure in uncovered piles lost over a year 3% of solids, 10% of nitrogen, 3% of phosphorus and 20% of potassium.
Covered piles and bottom-loading liquid systems with a surface crust conserve nutrients better; poultry manure may lose 50% of its nitrogen as ammonia unless protected.
Potassium is soluble, so a stack that lets water drain may lose much of it, since it sits mostly in the liquid portion.

definition.text: Anaerobic digesters process manure on large livestock farms to make biogas, mostly methane.

facts.text: The gas fuels on-farm heat and electricity or off-farm vehicles, and digesters can cut greenhouse gas emissions, odors and pathogens.
They are a major capital investment and may not pay without subsidies, energy, carbon credits, tipping fees and coproducts.
They separate liquid and solids but generally do not change total nutrient content, so excess nutrients and runoff remain.

definition.text: A high share of nutrients in feeds passes through animals into their manure, where it is available for recycling on cropland.

facts.text: Over 70% of nitrogen, 60% of phosphorus and 80% of potassium fed may be excreted as manure.
Manure also holds calcium, magnesium, sulfur and micronutrients; zinc deficiency is rare on soils regularly receiving manure.
Analyses vary widely by feed, supplements, bedding and storage, so manure should be analysed routinely; average liquid dairy manure holds about 25 pounds N per 1,000 gallons but may be 10 or 40.
About 10 tons of dairy solid manure or 4,000 gallons liquid supply 100 pounds N; poultry needs about 4 tons or 1,500 gallons.
Poultry manure is significantly higher in nitrogen and phosphorus than other types.

definition.text: Manure nitrogen occurs as ammonium, urea (soluble and quickly converted to ammonium) and solid organic N.

facts.text: Ammonium and urea are readily available but are lost as ammonia gas when left on a drying surface, with significant losses within hours.
Some manures have half to three-quarters of N in readily available form, others 20% or less; reports give ammonium and total N, the difference being mostly organic N.
Cattle manure is fairly balanced between available and organic N, while swine manure N is mostly ammonium or urea.

definition.text: Equal amounts of different manures affect soil organic matter differently, depending on how much solid is returned.

facts.text: Dairy and beef manures hold undigested forage and bedding rich in lignin, so they influence organic matter far more than unbedded poultry or swine manure.
Sand bedding and separating solids return less organic material to fields, whereas a bedded pack is high in solids.
With corn silage under conventional tillage, 20 to 30 tons of solid dairy manure per acre yearly maintain organic matter; less is needed if more residue returns.
20 tons of manure holds about 5,200 pounds of solids; mixed into the top 6 inches it would raise organic matter about 0.3%, but if 75% decomposes the net gain is 0.065%.
New York samples of 300 fields showed dairy-crop fields receiving manure averaged 0.5% higher organic matter than cash grain fields.
