title: Manure effects on soil properties

definition.text: Manure application causes biological, chemical and physical soil changes.

facts.text: In an 11-year Vermont continuous corn silage experiment, 20 tons of dairy manure yearly kept organic matter and CEC levels and close to the original pH, offsetting a monoculture's low residue return.
Dairy and poultry manures have a liming effect and counteract acidification.
Manured plots were better aggregated and less dense; organic matter was 5.2% originally, 4.3% unmanured and 5.2% at 30 tons, with pore space 44% versus 47%.
Liquid manure supplying the same N would not have raised organic matter, CEC and pore space nearly as much.

definition.text: Manure is usually applied at rates judged to supply the current crop's nitrogen.

facts.text: Common dairy rates are 10-30 tons solid or 4,000-11,000 gallons liquid per acre, supplying about 50-150 pounds available N; small grains need 10-15 tons, corn 20-30 tons.
Higher rates may build organic matter but risk nitrate buildup in leafy crops, nitrate leaching, salt damage and excess soil phosphorus.
Where soil P is far above optimum, apply by crop P need and export part of the manure.
Manure on legumes is discouraged because the legume then fixes less N, though it can suit intensive animal farms with excess N.
Manure P and K availability resembles fertilizer; 20 tons of dairy manure give about 30-50 pounds phosphate and 180-200 pounds potash.

definition.text: Ammonium and urea in manure left on the soil surface turn to ammonia gas as they dry and are lost to the air.

facts.text: About half of dairy manure N comes from urine urea, which converts to the ammonium that is almost all of its readily available N.
Surface-left dairy manure loses about 25% of its N after one day and 45% after four days, around 70% of the readily available N.
Half an inch of rain soon after application leaches ammonium in; incorporating the manure in spring helps, and fall injection of liquid manure greatly reduces loss compared with broadcasting.
Surface manure also risks nutrient runoff to surface waters.

definition.text: Manure is best applied near the time the crop needs nutrients.

facts.text: For annual crops apply in one dose just before tillage so it is incorporated fast; injection close to planting cuts runoff and erosion risk.

Fall application in humid climates lets ammonium convert to nitrate that leaches or denitrifies; a three-year New York study found about twice the N leaching from fall as from spring liquid manure on corn silage.
Grass hay, constantly N deficient, does best with about 50-75 pounds available N in early spring and after each harvest; wet early-spring soils risk compaction.
Spreading on frozen or snow-covered ground is legal in most states but poor practice; injection into a shallow 2-4 inch frozen layer avoids runoff.

definition.text: The share of the nitrogen in applied manure that a crop can use, which is hard to predict because nitrogen is the most dynamic nutrient.

facts.text: Phosphorus, potassium and most other manure nutrients stay in the soil and can be judged by soil testing, whereas manure nitrogen is easily lost with rain.
University and government guidelines give nitrogen availability factors, the fertilizer-N equivalent per pound of manure N; they suit planning but are imprecise because they ignore weather.
Spring applications use manure nitrogen better than fall or winter ones, since wet northeastern winters cause losses; the type of manure matters only modestly.
Prompt incorporation matters a great deal because much ammonia is lost from manure left on the surface, especially poultry and swine manure with more ammonium and urea than ruminant manure.
In the Penn State table, spring poultry manure incorporated immediately has a factor of 0.75 but only 0.15 if incorporated after more than 7 days or never.

A cover crop conserves fall and winter manure nitrogen by taking it up and returning it when terminated; analysis separating ammonia-N from organic N, and credits for earlier applications, refine the estimate.
Follow-up checks such as the pre-sidedress soil nitrate test, simulation models, remote imagery and crop sensors allow in-season correction of nitrogen.

title: Management intensive grazing

definition.text: A grazing system that rotates animals through many paddocks and does not regraze one until its plants have regrown.

facts.text: Continuous or rarely rotated pastures produce poorly because repeated grazing of early regrowth depletes root reserves and weakens plants.
Rotation cycles run from about a week or 10 days up to 6-8 weeks depending on season and weather; dairy cows may get a fresh paddock after every milking.

Harvesting and fertilizing need little equipment or labour, and electric fencing makes new paddocks quick to set up; intensively managed pasture often lowers production cost despite the animals' foraging energy.

Well-managed pasture combines perennial forage, no tillage and regular manure; New York soil health scores for organic matter, active carbon, respiration, water capacity and aggregate stability were far higher under pasture.
Stocking is about 100,000 pounds of animals per acre for 8-12 hours, used to suppress or kill poor plant species and let hooves help reseed more productive ones.
Where animals roam large rangeland by day and are stocked densely at night, the carbon, nutrients and seeds they gather are excreted into the small area, boosting fertility and revegetation.
Grazing crop residue after grain harvest cuts feed costs and improves nutrient and carbon cycling; cattle grazing corn residue in winter on the Great Plains raised soil health and yields.
Swath grazing leaves annual crops such as barley and triticale cut in swaths for beef cattle, which improves forage access under deep snow.

notes: Overlaps Managed grazing (Desertification#Better managed grazing), which covers the carbon-sequestration claims; this entry is the grazing practice itself.

title: Manure-driven nutrient buildup

definition.text: The accumulation of phosphorus and potassium in soil when manure is applied regularly at rates set by crop nitrogen need.

facts.text: Manure nutrient ratios are roughly equal to crop needs, about 2:1 nitrogen to phosphorus, so buildup is not caused by an unbalanced manure; it arises from nitrogen losses that force high rates.
Conserving nitrogen through timing, injection or incorporation lowers the manure rate needed, cutting P and K accumulation and the fertilizer N needed where P limits manure rates.

Erosion of P-rich topsoil carries sediment and phosphorus to streams and lakes; remedies include moving manure to other fields, soil conservation to trap sediment, and rotation crops like alfalfa that draw phosphorus down.
After many years the soil test P and K can reach excessive levels; all solutions need lower fertilizer P and P-containing amendments.
Remedies are exporting manure and using N fertilizer or legumes, spreading manure more evenly across fields, rotating to alfalfa, or sending manure to a neighbor or composting facility.

notes: Extends entry drafted in part11 (merge folds same title).

definition.text: A tool for assessing the risk of phosphorus moving from agricultural fields to surface water.

facts.text: It combines source factors such as soil test P, total soil P and the rate, method and timing of P application.
It also counts transport factors: sediment delivery, field position in the watershed, conservation practices, precipitation, runoff and tile drainage.
A nutrient planner uses it to rate P movement risk as low, medium or high and to suggest mitigation.

definition.text: Purchased feed brings nutrients onto a livestock farm that stay as manure, so a farm whose herd exceeds its land base accumulates them.

facts.text: Integrated crop-livestock farms that grow most of their feed keep nutrient imports and exports near balance.

Farms with animal numbers beyond their land's feed output risk nutrient buildup and groundwater and surface water pollution; options are sharing manure with neighbours, composting and selling it, or drying to ease transport.

definition.text: Animals on pasture drop excrement on the surface, making small concentrated nutrient spots between which soil is poorer.

facts.text: Some ammonium and urea is lost to the air as the pies dry, and dense vegetation keeps runoff low and N leaching less of a concern.
Because the patches are unevenly spread, nitrate leaching can still occur on intensively managed, fertilized dairy pasture.

definition.text: Building and tending a compost pile so that air, moisture and heat stay in the range where composting microbes work well.

facts.text: Oxygen moves into a pile while carbon dioxide, moisture and heat rise out, so it must pass air yet hold heat; bulking agents such as chips or chopped straw keep fine material open.
Settled piles are about 3-5 feet tall and 6-10 feet across at the base, wider in winter to hold warmth; sites must be accessible yet away from watercourses, wells, flood plains and homes.
Ideal moisture is about 40-60 percent, like a wrung-out sponge; at 35 percent or less ammonia escapes as gas and molds replace beneficial organisms.
Temperature is the main monitor: the most efficient range is 104-140 degrees F (40-60 C), though piles reach 170 F, and overheating kills beneficial organisms too.

Turning creates a new hot center, since lower sides barely compost; farm compost may need only one or two turns, and a pile heating uniformly needs none, while too much turning dries the pile and loses nitrogen and organic matter.

definition.text: The one to three month stage after hot composting, in which the pile cools and finishes its decomposition.

facts.text: Curing starts once temperatures drop to about 105 degrees F and no longer rebound after turning; a pile that reheats is not finished, and Solvita measures CO2 loss to judge maturity.
It further breaks down resistant chemicals and large particles, brings pH toward neutral, converts ammonium to nitrate, leaches soluble salts and lets common soil organisms colonize.
Moisture should stay at or below about 50 percent, and the early curing processes are thought to give compost some of its disease-suppressing quality.

definition.text: Composting in pits or closed vessels instead of open piles, for dry climates or small, controlled operations.

facts.text: Small farmers in developing countries, especially in dry and hot climates, dig compost pits; covering them with soil keeps animals out and retains moisture.
Home composters use vessels for easier turning, better temperature and moisture control and rodent exclusion, but vessels are generally not economical at commercial scale.

definition.text: Composts can suppress root and leaf diseases of plants, according to research by Harry Hoitink and coworkers at Ohio State University.

facts.text: Plants become healthier because microorganisms produce plant hormones and chelates that make micronutrients more available, so they resist infection better.
Beneficial organisms compete with pathogens for nutrients, consume them or produce antibiotics, and springtails and mites devour pathogen propagules.
Composts rich in biodegradable organic matter support microbes that induce systemic resistance in plants against root and leaf diseases.

Composts rich in available nitrogen can stimulate phytophthora root rot, fusarium wilt and fire blight; applying them months ahead, leaching salts or blending with low-nitrogen compost lowers the risk.

definition.text: Composted material is less bulky than the feedstock, so it is cheaper to transport and nicer to handle.

facts.text: The pile shrinks by 30-60 percent as carbon dioxide and water escape; heat kills many weed seeds and pathogens, odors and flies decline, and compost has about half the bulk and weight of manure.
Composting removes the nitrogen drawdown that follows adding sawdust or straw to soil, reduces nutrient solubility and stream pollution, and helps lower antibiotic levels in manure.
Compost stores easily for application when conditions are right, and lets farms with excess manure move nutrients to fields, gardens and landscapes that need them.

Direct addition of residues can be better: fresh residues stimulate more aggregate-binding gums, supply more readily available nutrients and cost less labour and energy; composting suits hard-to-handle, unsafe or odorous feedstocks, long hauls, pathogen concerns or good markets.

definition.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus behave very differently in soils, which shapes how each is supplied, lost and managed.

facts.text: Nitrogen comes mainly from decomposing organic matter and can be added biologically by legumes, but no biological process adds phosphorus, which also comes from soil minerals.
Nitrate, the main form plants absorb, is very mobile, whereas phosphorus movement is very limited and its available form is a small dissolved amount, mainly H2PO4- and HPO4 2-.
Most N loss is nitrate leaching, denitrification or ammonia volatilization; leaching dominates in sandy soils and denitrification in heavy loams and clays.
Phosphorus is lost mainly in runoff and eroded sediment, but low losses have a high effect per unit on water quality because P often limits freshwater algae.
P leaching matters in artificially drained fields: after years of excess manure or compost, P-saturated sandy soils leak P, and liquid manure can flow through wormholes and cracks to drain lines.
Cover crops store nitrogen that would otherwise leach, and mobilize P through mycorrhizae and store it for the next crop.
Excess N pollutes water with nitrate, raises nitrous oxide from denitrification, wastes energy in manufacture, speeds loss of soil organic matter and is linked to more insect damage.
Making, hauling and applying N fertilizer is about 30 percent of the energy used to grow corn.

definition.text: The higher the percent nitrogen in compost or another organic amendment, the larger the share of that N that becomes available to plants.

facts.text: An amendment with about 2 percent N or less (high C:N) supplies little to no available N, at about 5 percent N roughly 40 percent is available, and at 10-15 percent N 70 percent or more is available.
Fertilizer should supplement what soil organic matter, manure, compost and rotation or cover crops supply; organic farmers try to meet all demands from these sources.

definition.text: Available soil nitrogen depends on recent weather, so crop need for supplemental N fertilizer shifts from year to year.

facts.text: Mineral N rises in spring but falls in a wet spring as leaching and denitrification exceed conversion to mineral forms; a drier spring leaves more.
Mineralization, leaching and denitrification vary with organic matter, amendments, soil temperature (warmer means more mineralization) and wetness (saturated warm soils lose much N).

Seedlings take up little N at first, then rapidly, so an unusually wet spring may need extra sidedress N; Minnesota corn trials 2015-2019 gained an average of 11 bushels an acre in a quarter of cases from sidedress N.
Dry years lower yields and N need, but a drought at pollination cannot be foreseen at sidedress time.
Soil tests work well for P because plant-available P is strongly adsorbed, whereas N tests cannot give all answers.

title: Fixed and adaptive nitrogen recommendations
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.02%3A_Management_of_N_and_P#Fixed and Adaptive Methods for Estimating Crop N Needs

definition.text: Methods to estimate crop N needs fall into fixed approaches, which ignore season-to-season weather, and adaptive approaches, which adjust with field data, sensors or models.

facts.text: The mass-balance approach, the most common, takes N uptake for a yield goal minus credits from soil organic matter, preceding crops and amendments, but yield and optimum N rate are only weakly related in humid regions.
Fixed methods suit drier climates but are very imprecise in humid ones.
Pre-plant nitrate and labile N tests, measured early in the season, work better in drier climates such as the Great Plains but cannot include seasonal weather.
Leaf chlorophyll meters and satellite, aerial, drone or tractor sensors assess canopy N status to guide sidedress N, and simulation models use radar rainfall and soil databases.

title: Maximum return to nitrogen
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.02%3A_Management_of_N_and_P#Fixed and Adaptive Methods for Estimating Crop N Needs

definition.text: A fixed nitrogen recommendation method, used for corn, based on the rate with the largest average net return over many field trials.

facts.text: It draws on extensive field trials, model fitting and economics, and recommendations vary with grain and fertilizer prices.
Because it generalizes over large areas and many seasons, it ignores soil and weather effects and is imprecise for an individual field.

title: Pre-sidedress nitrate test
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.02%3A_Management_of_N_and_P#Fixed and Adaptive Methods for Estimating Crop N Needs

definition.text: A soil test of nitrate in the top 0-12 inches in late spring that guides sidedress or topdress nitrogen.

facts.text: It implicitly captures early-season weather and is especially good at identifying sites that need no more N fertilizer.
It needs special sampling in a short late-spring window and is sensitive to timing and early-spring mineralization; in the US Midwest it is called the late spring nitrate test.
It was the first approach to address dynamic N processes, giving more precise recommendations and cutting unnecessary N applications.

title: End-of-season nitrogen evaluation
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.02%3A_Management_of_N_and_P#Evaluation at the End of the Season

definition.text: Checks made after harvest to see whether the nitrogen rate used was too low, about right or too high.

facts.text: Farmers plant field strips at different N rates and compare yields, or sample soil nitrate after harvest in a 'report card' assessment of residual available N.
The lower stalk nitrate test also shows whether corn N rates were right, too low or too high, guiding rates in following years.

definition.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus need similar management strategies even though they behave differently in soil: count all sources, test, time and place applications, and keep soil covered.

facts.text: Take all nutrient sources into account, using soil, manure and compost tests, crop residue N, and the 4R principles of right rate, time, place and source, plus conservation practices.
Place fertilizer below the surface, split N applications where leaching or denitrification threaten, and apply when leaching and runoff threats are minimal.

Cover crops with minimal or no tillage improve structure, cut leaching, runoff and denitrification, and store N and P in organic form between cash crops; reduced tillage also keeps mycorrhizal networks intact for P.
Sod-type forage crops in rotation reduce nitrate leaching and P runoff, and grass cover crops such as cereal rye capture leftover nitrate.
Time N close to crop uptake; holding most fertilizer until a PSNT, sensor or model shows need lets sidedress N be applied only if wanted.

definition.text: Nitrogen fertilizer decisions should subtract the N supplied by manure, decomposing sods and legume or cover crops.

facts.text: Example credits (pounds per acre): corn 0; soybeans 0-40; 2-year clover 70; 3-year alfalfa 70 (20-60% legume) or 120 (>60%); crimson clover, winter peas and excellent hairy vetch 110.
Credits are the N available to the crop, not the total in residue; sandy soils get less, and cover crop growth stage and amount matter strongly.
High-yielding legume covers such as hairy vetch and crimson clover can supply most or all of the N for the next crop; many labs do not ask about cover crops.

title: Corn nitrogen efficiency
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.03%3A_Planning_for_N_and_P_Management#Reducing N and P Losses > New Technology For Corn Nitrogen Fertilization

definition.text: Corn turns each extra pound of absorbed N into more yield than most crops, yet corn systems typically use fertilizer N at under 50 percent efficiency.

facts.text: Leaching, denitrification and runoff losses are much higher for corn than for soybeans or wheat, and especially than alfalfa and grass, owing to growth cycle, rates, timing and rooting depth.
Many farmers add 'insurance' N for wet years though they may need it only about one season in four.

title: Surface broadcasting in no-till
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/19%3A_Management_of_Nitrogen_and_Phosphorus/19.03%3A_Planning_for_N_and_P_Management#Reducing N and P Losses > Tillage, Nutrient Loss, And Fertilizer Application Methods

definition.text: Broadcast fertilizer covers 500-800 acres in eight hours against about 200 for injection, but in no-till it risks nitrogen and phosphorus losses.

facts.text: After intense storms, surface urea on no-till soil can wash into wormholes and deep into the subsoil, so N should not be broadcast and left on the surface; residue urease speeds urea conversion to ammonia gas.
P accumulates on no-till surfaces and dissolved P in runoff is often higher than from tilled soil, so P should be applied below the surface.

title: Managing high-phosphorus soils

definition.text: High-P soils result from excessive P fertilizer or, more often, heavy manure use, and they need managing to limit phosphorus loss to water.

facts.text: They are common on livestock farms with limited land and imported feed, where feed nutrients exceed those exported in animal products, and where manure or compost applied to meet N adds extra P.

Risk depends on context: sites near critical water with slope, fine texture, poor structure or poor drainage need aggressive measures, while flat, grass-bordered vegetable or urban plots pose far less risk.

First cut P in animal diets (a survey found US dairy herds fed about 25% more P than NRC advice), then stop extra P by spreading manure on more land, swapping fields, or using legume covers and forages for N.
Do not use a high-P source such as compost to supply N, since P builds up over the long term.
Reduce runoff and erosion with reduced tillage, contour strips, cover crops, grassed waterways and buffers; tile drainage can still carry P, especially after heavy liquid manure.
Soil-test P falls slowly once imports stop, so test every two to three years; a one-time tillage can redistribute P built up at the surface of no-till soil, followed by starter P and injected manure.
A survey found the average US dairy herd was fed about 25 percent more P than the National Research Council recommends.
The extra supplemental P can cost thousands of dollars for a 100-cow herd and ends up as a potential pollutant.
